Photonic chips use light instead of electrons to process data

"Photonic chips are on the verge of a breakthrough," says Ton van Mol of the Dutch research institute TNO.

If van Mol is right – and TNO, the European Union and the Dutch government are backing the idea with millions of euros - then the technology could be a gamechanger.

The chips which run today's society, from your phone and TV, to the vast data centres meeting our insatiable desire for AI, are mostly electrical.

They process data by shunting electrons around tiny circuits – a single microchip produced today can contain billions of transistors, and sizes are measured in nanometres (one nanometre is a billionth of a metre).

Because they use light instead of electricity, photonic chips are faster, use less energy and generate less heat than traditional computer chips.

Van Mol hopes for an acceleration in photonics similar to the one seen in electrical chips since the 1970s.

"With optical chips, you are now where electronic chips were maybe 40 [or] 50 years ago."

American, Taiwanese and Chinese firms dominate the computer chip industry, but Europe sees the emergence of photonic chips as a fresh opportunity to lead, on what could be, a key future technology.

Which is why the European Union has committed €400m ($450m; £330m) to a project called PIX Europe , external , with the stated goal of making the continent "a global leader in emerging technology for Photonic Integrated Chips".

"Europe said 'we need to have our own manufacturing in-house'," says van Mol, who is leading a key part of the programme.

"We cannot depend like in the past that everything is manufactured in the US or China - that's not wise, so the [European] Chips Act was called into life, and one of the parts of the act is to build pilot lines to really bring the technology, which is now in labs, to the next stage - manufacturing."

Electronic and photonic chips are produced on wafers made up of hundreds of individual chips. Factories with machines that can handle bigger wafers can churn out chips more efficiently.

"[Photonic chip] manufacturing worldwide is [currently] done on wafers which are four inches (10cm) in size, and the next step is to scale-up production to a six-inch wafer," says van Mol.

His team are already building a 10,000 sq m factory to produce six-inch indium phosphide wafers on the High Tech Campus in the Dutch city of Eindhoven.

It's due to fully open in 2030 and will be a major step forward, not just for photonics in Europe, but around the world, according to van Mol.

"That's the development TNO is going to do, in a pilot line which is really serious.

"In 2030, we hope that we have a stable, reproducible, high-yield process, and then the intention is that the pilot line [opens] to industrial parties who can make commercial production out of it."

Netherland's based ASML is a crucial supplier of chip-making equipment

Europe does have one crucial player in the current computer chip industry - ASML.

The Netherlands-based tech giant is the only company in the world able to build the machines needed to make the most sophisticated semiconductors.

Which is why ASML products will sit at the heart of the pilot line in Eindhoven - it's no coincidence that van Mol's project is based around the corner from ASML's headquarters.

"The way you produce these [photonic] chips is very similar to the way you produce electrical or electronic chip," says van Mol.

"You use the same type of equipment, you also need a high-end clean room, you also use wafers, so the production method is very similar to the traditional semiconductor technology."

ASML itself is keen to explore the opportunities that the emerging technology of photonics could offer.

"Europe has a strong position in photonics research. The next challenge is translating those innovations into industrial-scale manufacturing," says Stanislas Baron, who is the head of ASML's EU/US Customer Team.

Peter Wennik says TNO's pilot production line is a "launchpad" for European tech

ASML's unique success has helped build an influential and lucrative network of companies and institutions devoted to semiconductor technology in and around Eindhoven, and it's a model for what Europe is trying to achieve with photonic chips.

The Eindhoven project has the backing of former ASML chief executive Peter Wennink, author of an influential report for the Dutch government called The Roadmap to Future Prosperity , external , which noted that the market for photonics was expected to grow 10 to 20 times in the next 10 years.

In a news release backing the new pilot line, Wennink described it as "a launchpad for Europe's future digital economy".

"By investing in scalable production capacity, we are creating an ecosystem that can help shape the global technological direction," he said.

Of course, Europe is not alone in looking to the potential of photonics to earn a global economic advantage.

In June this year, US photonics company Coherent , external announced what it called "the world's first and largest volume-production six-inch indium phosphide manufacturing platform" at its plant in Sherman, in Texas.

The expansion is backed by chip manufacturing giant Nvidia, as well as $50 million public funds under the US Chips Act.

It's an illustration of how quickly the market is moving, and how central photonic chips could be to the continuing race to retain an influential stake in AI and technological development more generally.

Europe's bid to establish itself as a global leader in photonic chips – exemplified by the Eindhoven project – is the kind of strategy that makes sense in a globalised economy, says Joris Teer, policy analyst at the European Institute for Security Studies in Brussels.

If the continent can take a lead in photonic chips, then future developments in AI and data will partly be dependent on Europe.

"Europe knows that its high energy and labour costs, skilled workforce shortages, and lack of private and public capital make an across-the-board reindustrialisation strategy impossible", Teer says.

"To retain influence, ensuring dependence on European parties rather than European autonomy is key."

Once up and running, the Eindhoven project will provide a pilot production line which can be used multiple companies.

It will be open to businesses across Europe and beyond, who can design and build chips without having to develop their own expensive production facilities.

"What we want to establish here is what we call a foundry model; there's no intention to have our own product," Ton van Mol says.

Instead, they will produce to order for outside customers.

It's the same idea which, at huge scale, has brought Taiwanese-based giant TSMC a position of global dominance in the manufacture of microchips.

Photonic chips are already in use, in highly specialised areas in data centres and in Lidar (light detection and ranging) sensor technology, for instance.

For van Mol of TNO, helping the industry to scale up, by easing production challenges and increasing capacity, is the key step to moving them into the tech we use in our daily lives, like phones and laptops, and to drive innovation in areas like medical scanners and 6G communications.

"The demand is there", says van Mol, "and the end goal is to have, in Europe, manufacturing of these chips, which is strategically very important because these chips [could] become the backbone of all data and telecom."

Current rules say all new cars must be zero emission by 2035

The UK is likely to miss legally binding climate targets if the government reduces electric vehicle (EV) targets, independent adviser the Climate Change Committee (CCC) has warned.

In a letter to Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander, the CCC argues that weakening the targets would result in "economic and energy security costs" and leave households "more exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices".

The CCC says that switching to an electric vehicle can save a typical household around £800 a year, with fewer people benefiting if the targets were watered down.

The warning comes after weeks of speculation that the government plans to announce changes to the EV targets. Government sources insist no decision has been made.

Under the current rules, a "zero emission vehicle" (ZEV) mandate requires 80% of new cars sold in the UK to be zero emission by 2030 and all new cars to meet that standard by 2035. Companies that fail to meet their ZEV mandate face a potential fine of £12,000 per car, although there are exemptions.

Industry groups have long complained the current rules impose too heavy a burden, calling instead for a "sustainable transition".

Latest data from trade body the Society of Motor Manufacturing and Traders (SMMT) shows that EVs, as well as plug-in hybrids, are driving growth in new car sales.

In the year so far, 26.6% of all new car registrations have been fully electric, the SMMT says, which is below the headline target of 33% for 2026.

But the industry as a whole appears on course to comply with this year's mandate once flexibilities are accounted for, according to analysis by New AutoMotive, a transport research organisation which supports the transition to electric cars

SMMT Chief Executive Mike Hawes accused the CCC of ignoring the costs of the targets it was defending.

"The industry cannot subsidise the transition indefinitely, which is why it is unified in seeking change," he said.

The CCC analysis also argued that weakening the targets would lead to a hole in the government's carbon savings that need to be made in order to meet its legally binding climate targets.

The CCC said the ZEV mandate "underpins the largest share of emissions reduction to 2037" in the government's net-zero plan. The climate targets set for 2033-2037 will be missed "without alternative action at the same scale", the CCC argued.

CCC analysis shows surface transport - which includes cars, vans and trucks - remains the country's highest carbon-emitting sector and one of the slowest to decarbonise.

Lord Deben, former CCC chairman, said going against CCC advice would "not be sensible" as it would "cost people money".

He said climate targets were "not random targets" and "if you don't reach them then you put yourselves in really serious danger of having climate change, which we can't handle".

A government spokesperson said: "We remain committed to the phase out of all new petrol and diesel cars by 2030 and to all new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, as well as to our legally binding net zero targets. Our consultation on the Mandate will not change this and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition."

Adverts for tests and services relating to low testosterone are allowed but most be rooted in evidence, the regulator said

Five adverts by online healthcare provider Voy have been banned by the watchdog for making misleading claims linked to low testosterone in men.

The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) said the adverts promoted Voy's at-home testosterone blood tests in three posters and two paid-for Facebook ads.

It said they were misleading as they linked common symptoms such as irritability and fatigue to low testosterone.

Voy said it had withdrawn the adverts while the investigation was under way and would not run them again.

The NHS says that while testosterone levels in men fall as they age, this is "unlikely" to cause any problems in itself.

It adds , external that while a testosterone deficiency in later life can sometimes be responsible for symptoms such as depression, loss of sex drive, erectile dysfunction, and other physical and emotional symptoms, they are often not linked.

Voy is a company that sells products such as testosterone, menopause and weight loss treatments.

Some of its testosterone test kit adverts drew a backlash online earlier this year when they appeared on the London Underground.

Some described them as "ragebait" for using phrases such as "It's not him, it's his hormones" and "Men get hormonal too".

At the time Voy said it was trying to destigmatise conversations about men's health.

Some of the adverts sparked discussion online after appearing at Tube stations

The ASA's ruling, however, took issue with how some of the adverts "exaggerated the connection between several common symptoms, which can have many possible causes, and low testosterone".

The ASA gave examples such as low sex drive, low energy, loss of motivation and changes in mood.

"While some symptoms may be more closely associated with the condition, others were much less specific and shouldn't have been presented as strong indicators of low testosterone in isolation," the watchdog said.

It added that one of the Facebook adverts also included the claim that "low testosterone sneaks up on 1 in 4 men over 30".

The ASA said this was misleading and not supported by the evidence provided by Voy.

Dr Earim Chaudry, chief medical officer for Voy, said: "Every patient decision at Voy is clinician-led and these campaigns were developed to align with UK advertising standards. We keep all our advertising under continual review to ensure it meets any updated guidance."

Wednesday's ruling followed two others in August by the watchdog, which found misleading claims in adverts for testosterone testing services from online providers BioID Health and Numan Digital Healthcare.

The rulings form part of a wider ASA investigation into adverts aimed at men concerned about their health.

This has identified a "recurring theme of advertisers playing on insecurities around libido, erectile problems, testosterone and ageing", the regulator said.

The watchdog said adverts for tests and services relating to low testosterone were allowed, but businesses needed to make sure the claims they made were accurate and supported by evidence.

Dr Richard Quinton, who is an expert in testosterone deficiency, said: "It's very easy to get a low testosterone level in any healthy man, simply by doing a blood test in the afternoon, after a meal, when unwell from any cause, or after an all-night sit up."

Waymo has temporarily suspended its driverless vehicles from operating on all US freeways, the company has said.

The decision comes after California banned Waymo's driverless taxis from state freeways following a series of recent traffic incidents.

California's Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) cited an "imminent hazard to public safety" for the ban, noting an incident this month in which several driverless Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on US Route 101.

Waymo said it was working with state officials "diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations", adding that no injuries or collisions were reported following the incident on US Route 101 south of San Francisco.

California's DMV said Waymo's driverless taxis presented a risk "due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present".

In another incident earlier this month, footage widely seen on social media appeared to show a Waymo car trying to overtake patrol vehicles that were deliberately slowing the pace of traffic on a San Francisco highway.

The California ban, which came into effect on 11 November, would remain in place until Waymo "demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions".

A Waymo spokesperson said: "In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance."

Data on Waymo's website suggests that its cars, compared to human drivers, are involved in 95% fewer crashes resulting in serious injury.

Waymo currently operates driverless taxis in 15 US cities, but only offered freeway rides in a handful of those locations, including San Francisco, Los Angeles and Miami.

The company's driverless taxis can continue to operate on regular city streets.

In May, Waymo recalled thousands of its self-driving cars in the US over a software issue that could allow vehicles to drive into flooded roads.

In the same month, multiple Waymo cars were spotted driving around a cul-de-sac in Atlanta, Georgia , in the early hours of the morning.

Watch: Jeff Bezos on involvement in casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond

Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has said he was "heavily involved" in picking actor Robert Pattinson for the role of James Bond in the next 007 film.

Speaking onstage at an event in California, the Amazon CEO said he was originally "biased against" Pattinson - who starred in a number of blockbuster films including Batman and the Twilight franchise - "because he's already so famous".

The role has typically gone to an actor who is not as well-known at the time of casting. But Bezos said in screen tests, "it was so obvious he is James Bond".

This will be the first 007 not under creative control of the Broccoli family, who has overseen the franchise since its start in 1962. Amazon purchased MGM in 2022.

'Good Bond vibes' - Hollywood locals react to Robert Pattinson cast as new 007

"There was something special about Rob", Bezos said at Semafor Silicon Valley & The World Event on Tuesday.

Pattinson was unveiled as the franchise's seventh James Bond on Monday, taking over from actor Daniel Craig. He will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028.

In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."

The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.

The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment.

Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.

But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands.

The pick comes amid widespread Hollywood cuts and consolidation, with studios struggling to get people into cinemas.

Hollywood insiders have said Pattinson was viewed as a safe pick to bring audiences in, rather than taking a risk on a new actor who could grow with the franchise.

"Maybe he's boring. Maybe Hollywood would be passing up a chance to anoint a badly needed new star. But with so much at stake for everyone involved, that all makes him the obvious pick," Hollywood journalist Matthew Belloni, who predicted the pick, wrote in his newsletter.

The BBC's Regan Morris contributed to this report.

MN202611_1i0v7nfnsrd.t: Imirwano i Bunyakiri muri teritwari ya Kalehe mu ntara ya Kivu y’Epfo mu burasirazuba bwa Repubulika ya Demokarasi ya Congo (RDC) yahungabanyije serivisi z’ubuvuzi ndetse ituma abasivili bata ingo zabo, nkuko bivugwa n’umuryango w’abaganga batagira umupaka, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF). MSF yabivuze mu itangazo yasohoye ku wa kabiri, ivuga ko imirwano hagati y’umutwe w’inyeshyamba wa FRN – wahoze witwa AFC/M23 – n’ingabo za leta (FARDC) yakajije umurego kuva ku itariki ya 6 y’uku kwezi kw’Ugushyingo (11). MSF ivuga ko ibintu byarujijeho kuba bibi ku wa gatanu nyuma y’ibitero by’indege nto z’intambara zitajyamo umupilote (zizwi nka ‘drones’) hafi y’i Bulambika, hegereye ibitaro bikuru bya Bunyakiri, bivura abaturage bava mu bice byinshi by’icyaro aho serivisi z’ubuvuzi zisanzwe zigera ku bantu bacye. Abakozi bo kwa muganga bimuye serivisi z’ubuvuzi, harimo n’abarwayi 76, babajyana ku kigo nderabuzima cya Maibano kiri hafi aho, mu gihe myinshi mu miti y’ibyo bitaro, ibikoresho hamwe n’ibindi byifashishwa kwa muganga byasigaye mu bitaro. MSF ivuga ko iryo hungabana ry’ubuvuzi rishobora kugira ingaruka ku bantu babarirwa mu bihumbi basanzwe bagana ibyo bitaro. Uwo muryango uvuga ko bamwe mu bakozi bawo na bo bataye ingo zabo, ndetse ko urimo kugerageza kumenya amakuru y’abakozi benshi bawo. MSF ivuga ko yabaye igabanyije ibikorwa byayo, yimura bamwe mu bakozi bayo ibajyana i Bitale n’i Bukavu, ahantu hasanzwe hibasiwe na kolera (cholera) n'ubwiyongere bwa malaria. Iyi ntambara irimo gutuma ibikorwa by’ubutabazi muri rusange bigorana mu burasirazuba bwa RDC. Amashami y’Umuryango w’Abibumbye na leta ya RDC bavuga ko intara ya Kivu y’Epfo ari imwe mu zibasiwe cyane no kutihaza mu biribwa, aho abaturage bagera kuri miliyoni 1.1 bahanganye n’ikibazo gikomeye cy’inzara, mu gihe intambara yagabanyije umubare w’abashobora kugera mu mirima yabo no mu bikorwa bisanzwe bibabeshaho. MSF ivuga ko haramutse habayeho ihungabana ry’igihe kirekire rya serivisi z’ubuvuzi, bishobora gutuma abantu babarirwa mu bihumbi bagera gacye kuri serivisi z’ubuvuzi, mu karere gasanzwe karimo kugorwa no guhangana n’indwara zinyuraye, abaturage bava mu byabo hamwe n’inzara. The Lobito Corridor links DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast through the Benguela Railway and the Port of Lobito

As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not thinking about critical minerals or billion-dollar investments.

She is thinking about getting around more easily.

The railway runs through Catumbela, near the Angolan city of Lobito, on the Atlantic coast.

For Julia, it has made travelling cheaper and more convenient.

"Before, I had to use a taxi, which is much more expensive. Now it is cheaper and easier to travel," she says.

But the railway has ambitions far bigger than improving local transport.

It is part of the Lobito Corridor, a US-backed effort to secure access to Africa's critical minerals and promote regional economic cooperation, which Washington hopes will help bring peace to conflict-torn eastern DR Congo.

Under agreements brokered by US President Donald Trump, DR Congo and neighbouring Rwanda have committed to greater economic cooperation, including more transparent mineral supply chains and regional infrastructure development.

The wider plan envisages linking these initiatives to the railway, which transports minerals from Central Africa to Western markets via Angola, rather than east to China as most do currently.

The hope is that formalising the mineral trade and encouraging investment could help curb illicit markets that have helped finance armed groups and fuel instability.

Manuela Julia says the railway has made travelling around easier

But can a railway built to move minerals to global markets also deliver peace and prosperity?

The Lobito Corridor links DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast through the Benguela Railway and the Port of Lobito.

Its importance has grown as demand for copper and cobalt rises, driven partly by the global transition to cleaner energy, as both are critical ingredients for all kinds of electrical components.

"The timing matters," says Johannesburg-based political risk analyst Wellington Muzengeza

"Electrification and the energy transition have increased the strategic importance of copper, cobalt and reliable mineral supply chains."

DR Congo is the world's largest producer of cobalt and one of its biggest copper producers, along with neighbouring Zambia. The US sees the corridor as a means to diversify mineral supplies and reduce reliance on China, which dominates much of the world's processing capacity.

A US-DR Congo strategic partnership identifies the route from the Congolese town of Sakania to Lobito as a priority for mineral exports, while the economic framework agreed by DR Congo and Rwanda envisages connecting regional infrastructure and trade initiatives to the corridor.

The project has attracted over $750m (£570m), including funding backed by the US International Development Finance Corporation and the Development Bank of Southern Africa to upgrade railway tracks, signalling systems and trains.

The railway, built in 1902 under Portuguese colonial rule, was originally designed to transport goods and minerals from Central Africa to the Atlantic coast. After years of disruption during Angola's civil war, it was rebuilt and fully reopened in 2015.

The US first got involved in the project under former President Joe Biden but backing has continued under Trump.

At Lobito's mineral terminal, the renewed ambitions are already visible.

When the BBC visited, a train carrying about 12,000 tonnes of copper cathodes from DR Congo had arrived. Workers moved the refined copper sheets into a warehouse before they were loaded on to ships bound for international markets, mostly the US.

The cargo is handled by Lobito Atlantic Railway (LAR), which has a 30-year concession to operate freight services along the corridor and manage the mineral terminal.

The Lobito Atlantic Railway has a 30-year concession to operate freight services along the corridor

Chief operating officer Nicholas Gregoir says freight volumes have more than doubled since the company took over in January 2024.

LAR expects to transport about 200,000 tonnes of copper through the corridor in 2026.

For mining companies, the railway offers a shorter route to international markets.

"The Lobito Corridor is the shortest route for both Zambia and the DRC," to the Atlantic, says Kátila Vanessa Monteiro da Silva Neto, executive director of the Lobito Port Authority.

Zambia, Africa's second-largest copper producer, also plans to connect its Copperbelt to Lobito through a proposed 830km (515 mile)-railway.

But a more efficient route to market does not automatically translate into economic transformation.

"Joining a corridor is not the same as industrialising," Muzengeza says. "The test is not simply whether Zambia gains another route to the sea. It is whether that route helps build a stronger economy."

Some Angolans believe the railway's greatest value could lie in what it offers businesses and communities beyond mining.

"I call it a corridor of development," says businessman Adérito Areias.

The railway passes through some of Angola's most productive agricultural regions.

Better transport links could help farmers reach larger markets and reduce losses.

"If there isn't an artery carrying products from the interior to where there is demand, those products simply rot where they are produced," Areias says.

But the challenge is turning that ambition into reality.

The Port of Lobito handled about 1.8 million tonnes of cargo in 2025, of which around 158,000 tonnes was minerals. Its mineral terminal can handle up to 3.6 million tonnes annually.

"The port already has the capacity," says Neto. "What we need now is sufficient railway capacity and rolling stock."

For residents along the route, the benefits have been immediate.

State-owned railway operator Caminho de Ferro de Benguela (CFB), which runs passenger services, carried a record 1.6 million passengers in 2025.

LAR says it directly employs nearly 1,000 people, 98% of them Angolan.

"This job allows me to support my family," says Domingos Canhama, a father of four and a forklift operator at CFB.

"I can put food on the table, maintain a home and help support my father," he says.

Muzengeza argues that the bigger opportunity is developing local businesses in engineering, maintenance, warehousing and agricultural processing.

"Businesses in Angola need access to the railway, not just proximity to it. That means feeder roads, electricity, storage and predictable services," he says.

But can minerals and their movement along the railways line help deliver peace to eastern DR Congo, where the battle for control of mineral resources has fuelled decades of conflict?

Domingos Canhama, a forklift operator at the Lobido railway company says the job has helped him support his family

Most recently, this has seen the M23 rebel group seize control of many mineral-rich areas.

The Congolese government says neighbouring Rwanda is backing the M23 in order to gain access to DR Congo's mineral wealth. Despite overwhelming evidence, Rwanda denies backing the M23.

The Trump-backed agreements between DR Congo and Rwanda seek to promote transparent mineral supply chains, cross-border investment and regional infrastructure, with the aim of ensuring mineral wealth does not finance armed groups.

"The US wants reliable access to minerals essential to defence, advanced technology and energy systems, while reducing dependence on supply chains in which China has substantial influence," says Muzengeza, the political risk analyst

"Lobito is therefore more than a railway but an infrastructure that can reshape trade routes and commercial power."

At a meeting in Paris in November, DR Congo urged the US to turn its strategic partnership into tangible investments, arguing that success should be measured by completed projects rather than signed agreements.

"We want the partnership to support ⁠local mineral processing, electricity access for households and businesses and peace in the east," said DR Congo's Economy Minister Daniel Mukoko Samba.

Even if more minerals move through formal channels, better infrastructure alone would not resolve the political and security tensions driving the conflict.

There is also the question of who captures the wealth. Much of the copper and cobalt transported from DR Congo through Lobito is destined for processing and manufacturing outside Africa.

While Angola can earn transit fees and create logistics jobs, much of the higher-value activity takes place elsewhere.

"When you export raw materials, you are also exporting jobs and knowledge," Angola's Foreign Affairs Minister Téte António tells the BBC.

"We should not export lithium but export batteries," he says, arguing that the corridor should help develop local processing and manufacturing rather than simply accelerate raw material exports.

Back in Catumbela, such debates can feel distant from everyday life.

For Julia, the railway already means cheaper journeys and easier movement.

But its ultimate success will depend on whether it can deliver more than faster mineral exports.

Whether it can also help secure lasting peace in eastern DR Congo, where the minerals are mined, remains the bigger test.

Recent tech outages across the US are "completely unrelated" to one another, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said.

Microsoft outlook went down for nearly an entire day, a tech glitch briefly grounded all flights in the US and major American banks reported system issues all in the space of several days.

The secretary said there is "zero evidence" of a link between the recent cyber incidents.

Rubio spoke to media in the Philippines' capital Manila, where he is joining US President Donald Trump on a major foreign event attending the Asean and Apec summits, where he is expected to meet with the leaders of China and Russia.

A tech start-up used AI to uncover a critical software bug in Java that had existed for more than a decade

A cyber-security firm has used artificial intelligence (AI) to uncover a major flaw in the hugely popular computer language program Java.

Tech start-up Calif - which recently identified a cyber-security flaw in another programming language, PHP - found the bug in Java's memory functions.

Java is the world's third largest programming language used by 90% of the world's Fortune 500 companies like Apple and Amazon, and many banks, hospitals and governments.

The discovery comes after a string of serious technology issues, including a massive Microsoft outage and a network failure that grounded all US flights. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there is 'zero evidence' the incidents are related .

More recently, the US National Security Agency said its internal communications went offline on Tuesday due to a "scheduled routine maintenance".

Apple also reported multiple services suffered full outages due to an internal update.

The NSA did not specify whether its outage was linked to the identified Java bug.

With the help of AI, Calif discovered a serious security vulnerability called Java4Shell, which allowed an adversary to remotely execute unwanted commands to Java's memory system.

That adversary was OpenAI's recently released model GPT-6 Cyber, which is not yet available to the public. But there are fears hackers could now identify the bug if the flaw isn't fixed.

Oracle, the owner of Java, has not acknowledged the bug, but released a "critical patch update" on Tuesday, which it said contained security vulnerability fixes. And at this stage it is unclear if any platforms or companies have been affected by the latest incident.

But the Java flaw remains a huge concern for cyber-security experts, who say overloading a system's memory is one of the most common ways for hackers to exploit or crash a system.

One of the main functions of Java is that it is supposed to manage and protect memory for you, Professor Toby Walsh, computer scientist and one of the world's leading researchers in AI, told the BBC.

"This is why this is such an unlikely and serious flaw," Walsh added. Java is meant to make the IT world more secure by managing your memory online, he said.

Anytime you transfer information on the internet, receive a file from a user or need to log into an IT system with a password, the platform you are using is likely relying on a Java program.

First released in 1995, the programming language and computing system is now the "beating heart of the modern economy", Calif said in its investigation.

Nearly every critical sector, including banking, national security systems, aviation and telecommunications, relies on Java.

It's a serious flaw that could comprise "critical financial systems, customers and organisation's data," cyber-security expert Dr Pedram Hayati said.

In Australia alone, almost every bank uses Java for managing critical transaction data, Hayati added.

As global security services or companies search for critical cyber-security flaws they are relying more on AI.

Earlier in November, OpenAI President Greg Brockman announced his company was pivoting 25% of its staff to focus on cyber-security demands.

The announcement followed a critical cyber-security flaw identified in the PHP programming language, identified by the same company Calif.

PHP is the code that websites like Wikipedia use to collect information and present it in a way you can read on the web.

Surrey Centre for Cyber Security Prof Alan Woodward said the PHP flaw affected some 30 million websites, leaving them vulnerable to malicious attacks.

At the time, website owners were urged to check if their sites were affected and, if so, they were told to install updates to patch the issue or consider going offline.

Earlier this week, thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, reported trouble accessing services.

The latest incidents have exposed how nearly every critical sector - including national security systems, aviation and telecommunications - rely on legacy infrastructure online.

The PHP flaws went undetected for at least a decade, which Walsh said is similar to what has happened with Java.

"It's been hiding in plain sight for 12 years", he said.

"AI is now exposing more flaws much more quickly," Walsh said including ones that may have been so obscure and difficult that humans could not have discovered them alone.

KIGALI – Rwanda’s hopes of ending their encounter with Mali on a positive note faded in the closing minutes on Tuesday evening, as the visitors secured a 2-0 victory that underlined the difference in depth and quality between the two sides.

The Amavubi struggled to find their rhythm in the first half, falling behind to a 27th-minute goal from Modibo Sagnan before mounting a much-improved challenge after the break.

But despite periods of sustained pressure, Rwanda could not find a way past Mali’s defence, and a late second goal from Gaoussou Diarra settled the contest, much to the disappointment of the home fans.

The opening exchanges were closely contested, with Rwanda initially keeping Mali at bay, and a defensive lapse nearly presented the visitors with an early opportunity before goalkeeper Fiacre Ntwari intervened.

Mali gradually grew into the game, and their pressure eventually produced the breakthrough just three minutes before the half-hour mark.

President Paul Kagame arrived at the stadium around the 10th minute, prompting loud cheers from supporters in the stands. The atmosphere remained lively as Rwanda sought to respond to the setback, but the hosts went into the break trailing by a goal.

In the second half, Head coach Stephen Constantine introduced Abeddy Biramahire for Gilbert Mugisha at the interval, and the Amavubi returned with greater urgency, pushing higher and committing more players forward.

Rwanda then began to create openings of their own. Joy-Lance Mickels came close in the 55th minute, while Ellie Tatou Iradukunda sent an effort wide as the hosts pressed for an equalizer.

The pressure intensified in the 65th minute, with Rwanda winning successive corners and forcing Mali to defend deep in their own half. The visitors, who had looked comfortable for much of the first half, were increasingly required to absorb attacks and protect their lead.

The Eagles remained disciplined at the back, and eventually found room to put the result beyond doubt when Diarra scored in the 87th minute. The Amavubi had another opportunity late on, but Mali’s goalkeeper held on to the ball as the match ended 2-0.

The result offered a reminder of the work Rwanda still needs to do to build a squad capable of competing consistently against established African teams.

Mali not only had quality in their starting line-up but also options from the bench to maintain their competitiveness as the match developed. Constantine acknowledged that difference, pointing to Mali’s younger squad and greater depth.

In a post-match press conference, he argued that Rwanda’s response cannot depend solely on changes to the senior team, but must begin with the structures that develop players long before they reach international level.

“We need to develop our young players because we have the talent in this country. Stronger grassroots programs, better coaching and more opportunities for young footballers to progress are extremely important,” Constantine said.

He also questioned the limited availability of academies at club level, arguing that the country needs to invest in developing players from an early age rather than expecting the national team to bridge the gap on its own.

Accepting that his side had not performed to its full potential in the opening half, he was, however, encouraged by the response after the break, when the Amavubi managed to put Mali under pressure for an extended spell.

Mali’s coach said his team had anticipated a difficult match and made tactical adjustments to deal with Rwanda’s attacking movement. He acknowledged that the hosts caused problems after the interval, forcing his players to retreat and defend for a sustained period.

“In football, no team anywhere in the world can control all 90 minutes. Our team had to adapt to Rwanda’s improved approach,” he said.

For the Amavubi, the defeat was another difficult result, but the second-half performance showed that the team could compete for periods against a side with greater depth in the upcoming final round of games.

The result leaves Rwanda second in Group K with six points after four matches, behind already-qualified Mali, who have 12. Liberia and Cape Verde are level on three points each following Liberia’s 2-0 victory over Cape Verde.

With two matches remaining in March 2027, Rwanda still have their qualification hopes in their own hands with a win in either of their remaining games, against Liberia and Cape Verde able to guarantee at least second place, securing a ticket to the 2027 AFCON finals.

Tees Rivers Trust workers have been tagging eels to track their downstream migration

Conservationists have spent summer and autumn searching for critically endangered eels to tag as they begin their downstream migration.

The Tees Rivers Trust have found 12 large eels by fyke netting, a method of catching eels with a cylindrical net, around the River Tees catchment.

The team managed to electronically tag 10 of them and the largest was 60cm (23ins) in length and weighted 435g (0.9lbs).

Project manager Ellie Ward said the eels caught this year were not as large as usual and were "harder to catch".

The team has been searching for "silver" eels which have finished maturing and are preparing to head back out to the Sargasso Sea near Bermuda.

Ward said: "European eels start to migrate downstream during autumn and winter, when river discharges increase.

"We suspect that low flows in summer that have continued into autumn have contributed to low catch rates so far this year."

The Eels of Steel project is funded by Natural England and the Tees Rivers Trust has been conducting the research alongside Hull University.

Each eel has a tag which emits a unique ping, which provides information about their movements while migrating.

The project aims to discover if the critically endangered animal is successfully leaving the river and making it through river barriers such as sluices and weirs.

Conservationists say it has been harder than usual to find the eels

Since 2008, European eels have been listed as critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

Numbers have declined by between 90-95% since the 1980s due to a range of factors including habitat loss, climate change and overfishing.

Ward said: "It is incredible to think about the journey these eels are embarking on, back to their spawning grounds in the Sargasso Sea.

"No-one has ever witnessed European eels spawning, they are a species that hold so much mystery."

The team say they are always open to suggestions for netting locations, particularly lakes and ponds, and ask people to contact them.

The BBC has been investigating whether discharges of treated sewage might be responsible for poor water quality at a bathing site in Taunton.

The official sign on the banks of the River Tone at French Weir Park in Taunton advises people not to swim.

But that hasn't stopped Jo, Jenny, Sue and a second Jo from enjoying a regular dip together.

"People think, oh you're swimming down by the supermarket, that can't be very nice, but it's gorgeous," Jenny Hillier says, as the women huddle round with their coats and hot drinks after a bracing October plunge.

People have been swimming at the spot on the River Tone in the centre of Taunton for more than a hundred years.

But it is only since 2024 that French Weir Park has been designated an official bathing site, which means from May to September the water gets tested by the Environment Agency (EA).

Those tests regularly confirm what the women's senses have been telling them for a while - the water quality is poor.

"There are times when we've come down and we haven't got in, either because of the look or the smell," says Jo Macdonald. "We don't take risks. We don't put our faces in. We don't swim with cuts or anything."

"This summer I got quite poorly," Jenny says, explaining that she'd had diarrhoea, vomiting and muscle cramps.

"I'd swum and then within six hours I was unwell. I was poorly for probably about seven to 10 days and it was not nice. I think it was the river that day."

"There are germs everywhere, all over the place. You can catch Covid in Tesco," she says.

Despite the high levels of faecal bacteria and the health warnings, Jenny, Jo and Jo have kept swimming at the bathing site in Taunton

This summer French Weir Park failed its tests on 13 of the 19 days it was sampled. The BBC analysed data from all four regulators across the UK for 2026 and found French Weir Park's failure rate of 68% was the highest of all the bathing sites

The regulators look for two types of faecal bacteria – E. coli and intestinal enterococci – that originate either in human or animal guts and can make people ill if ingested.

So where's it coming from at French Weir Park? The local water company Wessex Water says it could have come from wildlife, agriculture, private septic tanks as well as its sewerage works.

We decided to take a closer look to see if we could work out where the truth lies.

Our wastewater treatment system is built on the assumption that faecal bacteria - from our poo - once discharged into nature will be rapidly diluted and perish.

The bacteria are known to have little impact on wildlife but they can make humans sick if ingested – so the rise in popularity of wild-swimming and testing of bathing sites have increased awareness.

As part of a BBC investigation we analysed the water sampling results from this summer across all the UK's 700 official bathing sites on the coast, in lakes and rivers.

We found that more than 10% of the UK's coastal sites and 37% of its inland sites failed to meet regulators' minimum standards across the summer.

That difference is likely to be because the sea acts as a more effective dispersant and can dilute and kill faecal bacteria quicker than a lake or river.

Of the 11 worst bathing sites in England in 2026, seven were on inland rivers or lakes.

Last year the official advice was not to swim at 12 of the 14 inland river bathing sites in England .

Poor water quality has historically been linked to raw sewage spills. These are much more likely after it has rained. So why, in a summer that was extremely dry, did bacteria levels remain high in so many rivers?

In Taunton the official testing data suggests there has been a constant flow of bacteria entering the river.

So the BBC carried out its own sampling near three wastewater treatment works upstream of the Taunton site. We found the treated liquid coming out of the nearest sewage works at Bradford-on-Tone had about 240,000 colony forming units (CFU) of E. coli per 100ml - that's a level about 250 times higher than that considered safe for swimming.

"The counts from just outside the treatment works in my experience were high for treated effluent", Dr Rob Morley from Index Microbiology told us at his laboratory near Bristol as he peered down at small dots of E. coli bacteria on a transparent plastic plate.

What was of particular interest to Morley were the results of the test on water samples we'd taken above and below the point where the treated wastewater enters the River Tone.

It showed 199 CFU of E. coli above, which is fine for swimming and 7,701 CFU just below, more than eight times the regulators limit.

"You can see where it's seeding the river with pollution," Morley says.

"If we were to look further down the river, we would expect the levels to get lower with the dilution effect. But that does quite clearly show the impact that treated effluent can have on the river."

We shared our findings with Dr Andrew Thompson, a fellow at the Institute of Chemical Engineers. He was involved in a 2024 report that warned high concentrations of bacteria and viruses were common , external , particularly in the summer when river levels are lower and could cause serious diseases if ingested.

Thompson told the BBC the levels of E. coli we found in the River Tone were not illegal, or even particularly unusual, because there are currently no laws or regulations about how much bacteria water companies are allowed to discharge in what the industry calls treated effluent.

Dr Rob Morley of Index Microbiology assisted in analysing the water samples around the wastewater treatment works

We also wanted to know whether analysing the E. coli samples from the bathing site could give us clues to where it came from.

With assistance from researchers at the University of Bristol, Morley arranged for e-DNA analysis to be carried out to identify whether the E. coli bacteria were more likely to be from a human or animal gut.

The answer, as is often the case with water quality, is complex. There were lots of different types of E.coli in the samples.

"Some were from humans, some were from animals and some were just generic from the environment," Morley says. "It definitely suggests that some of the E. coli is definitely coming from human origins, therefore potentially from that treatment works."

As with all of our testing, more needs to be done to reach firm conclusions.

Both the EA and Wessex Water are investigating what's causing the water quality in Taunton to be so poor. But sources at the EA told the BBC that constant flows of treated effluent is high up the list of likely culprits.

In response to our testing Wessex Water told the BBC its treatment works at Bradford on Tone was working normally and was meeting all its permit conditions set by the EA.

So could steady flows of treated effluent loaded with bacteria be behind many of the problems at bathing sites across the UK?

"All the sewage treatment works in the UK and in England have permits to protect the ecology and the wildlife within the river," says Jim Flory, a regional manager for the EA in the south-west.

"They've not set permits for bathing water regulations, which are all about protecting people who may want to be swimming, canoeing or using the water."

That has led to a system where a popular bathing site gets officially designated – the testing regime discovers it has high levels of faecal bacteria – and then a lengthy process begins to try to work out where the sources are and whether it's affordable to fix them.

Tessa Fayers of Thames Water says installing UV disinfection, like they have at Cassington near Oxford, everywhere is just too expensive

Wolvercote Mill Stream in Oxford was the second inland river to get bathing water status in 2022 and since then the water has always been rated "poor".

In an attempt to improve things, banks of ultraviolet (UV) lights have just been installed at a cost of £4m upstream at Cassington wastewater treatment works to kill bacteria before they reach the River Thames. But there's no question of it being installed everywhere.

"The reality is it's expensive. We have to be sure we're spending money wisely," Tessa Fayers from Thames Water says.

UV disinfection has been installed at 160 of the nearly 7,000 wastewater treatment works across England – almost always as targeted interventions to protect either shellfish or bathing sites downstream.

Wessex Water said it had no plans to introduce UV disinfection at Bradford-on-Tone and that it would publish its conclusions on why the water quality is so poor in April 2027.

Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) spending boom.

No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.

That partnership has now ended following Huang's resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, one of which is alleged to have been with a Chinese spy.

The company has been rocked by the scandal, with hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value and questions swirling about the extent of the impact of Huang's departure.

While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.

The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.

Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.

It is now one the most valuable firms, worth $3.8 trillion (£2.9 trillion), and on Tuesday said its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.

But there's now an air of uncertainty over Nvidia's future direction. Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on the company, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him.

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at investment firm AJ Bell, says because Huang was also a key figure in "flying the flag" to drum up enthusiasm and investment for the wider AI industry, his departure posed a "real risk" that Nvidia could now decide to change its current strategy and rein in spending.

Such a move could spell a wider slowdown in AI investment, which would have an economic impact. How big? That's "unknown", Coatsworth says.

"If they decide to go with the much more cautious route... there could be a knock-on effect in that you have got various companies in the AI infrastructure space suddenly finding they don't have a key source of finance," he says.

Kunjan Sobhani, senior technology industry analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, expects the impact of Huang leaving to be "limited" for now as Nvidia has strong commitments and a deep order book. But he said this picture could change in the long run.

That is because Nvidia, on its journey to the top of the AI industry, has created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".

Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.

The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?

That risk is perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, have called for Huang's reinstatement.

Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, which has also prompted a campaign by shareholders and supporters to "Bring Jensen Back".

Huang himself has said he is open to a return just after a week after resigning .

Coatsworth says he has never seen circular financing used at this scale before, but admits there are competitive rivals around, which could insulate the wider AI industry from any potential slowdown at the firm.

When Nvidia's share price plunged in the wake of the affair revelations, the stock of its rival semiconductor makers including AMD, Broadcom and Marvell Technology jumped.

"I don't think all AI activity grinds to a halt if Nvidia slows down what it's doing and if it pulls some financing, but it does change how people would look at the whole situation," Coatsworth adds.

The risk of a slowdown has already rattled stock markets. Investors took fright at Democrat gains in the midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms.

Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will actually pay off.

Investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to Goldman Sachs, which said the technology will remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.

Nvidia's interim boss, Colette Kress, said it was "business as usual" without Huang at the helm as the company's rapid growth remains on track.

The value of the shares in Big Tech companies have cushioned the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs, buoying investments and pensions for people worldwide.

Despite Huang saying he would be "honoured" to return, Nvidia's board has said it is not considering bringing him back.

And while Coatsworth thinks "no CEO is irreplaceable", he admits the pressure is on for whoever succeeds him.

The move comes amid persistent security crises across Nigeria, including banditry, mass kidnappings and communal violence

Nigeria has moved a step closer to introducing state police system after all 36 states approved a motion to create and operate their own police force alongside federal police.

The resolution, which seeks to amend the constitution, now requires President Bola Tinubu's assent to become law. It also requires further federal and state legislation for state police to become operational.

The move comes amid persistent security crises across Nigeria, including banditry, mass kidnappings and communal violence, which the federal security forces have struggled to contain.

There are also concerns about the shortage of police officers, who rights groups say are often poorly equipped,inadequately trained and vulnerable to corruption in a country of more than 200 million people.

Nigeria currently has a centralised police system, with the federal government controlling the police under 1999 Constitution

On Tuesday, the Clerk to the National Assembly, Kamoru Ogunlana, said his office had completed the verification of resolutions submitted by state legislatures in support of the constitutional amendment.

He described the unanimous backing as 100% approval, exceeding the legal requirement of at least 24 states.

Under the proposed two-tier system, the federal police would retain responsibility for enforcing federal laws and protecting national institutions, as well as tackling threats such as terrorism, cybercrime and border security.

State police would be responsible for enforcing state laws, maintaining public safety and preventing and investigating offences within their jurisdictions.

The federal police would, however, be allowed to intervene in a state on some occasions including serious breakdown of public order or human rights violations.

Such intervention will however require presidential authorisation and will be subject to judicial review.

Supporters of the state police argue that decentralizing law enforcement would allow authorities to respond quickly to security threats and better understand local conditions.

But critics fear that governors could use the forces to intimidate political opponents, suppress dissent or influence elections.

The proposed law includes safeguards intended to prevent political interference and abuse of power.

Governors would be prohibited from ordering officers to unlawfully arrest or detain individuals or groups.

Independent state police commissions would oversee hiring, discipline and accountability. Their officials would be appointed by governors on the recommendation of the federal National Police Council.

Higher petrol and diesel prices pushed the UK's inflation rate up again last month, official figures show.

Prices rose 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5% in September, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.

Elevated oil prices also affected the wider economy, the ONS said, continuing to drive up the cost of raw materials and goods leaving factories.

Prices have surged in recent months because of the US-Iran war, with the Bank of England raising interest rates for the first time in three years earlier this month in a bid to slow price rises.

Interest rates increased from 3.75% to 4%, and the Bank signalled a further rate rise could be likely unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved.

Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the ONS, said fuel prices were "once again a major contributor" to the increase in the inflation rate in October.

Rising energy prices can lead to more expensive food and staples for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs.

Earlier this month, the Bank of England said there had been "limited evidence" of this, with some firms absorbing cost increases and accepting lower profit margins.

But Fitzner said on Wednesday: "Annual costs of both raw materials and goods leaving factories continue to climb, driven by higher crude oil and petrol prices, respectively."

Petrol prices rose by 5.2p per litre between September and October, the ONS said, with the average price last month hitting 174.7p per litre - the highest since August 2022.

Diesel prices, meanwhile, reached the highest price since records began 30 years ago, averaging 199.5p per litre in October.

The ONS said price inflation in restaurants and cafes had slowed last month, and that prices had fallen on average for hotels.

Elikia Mbinga made his Eredivisie debut for PEC Zwolle in September 2021

Elikia Mbinga dreamed of becoming a professional footballer and playing in sold-out arenas after captaining an Ajax side brimming with future stars.

But at 25, his life has taken an unexpected turn. Rather than showcasing his creativity on the pitch, Mbinga is making a name for himself through music.

He has become one of the most successful emerging afrobeat artists in the Netherlands, with more than 30 million Spotify streams.

It is a world away from Ajax's famed De Toekomst academy, where he trained alongside a host of Dutch talents who have since made their mark in the Premier League - from the Timber brothers to Ryan Gravenberch and Brian Brobbey.

It is clear the lessons Mbinga learned during his esteemed footballing education have helped shape his identity as an artist.

"As a footballer, I played in midfield and was a very creative player. That was my style on the pitch, and I try to bring that same creativity to my music," he tells BBC Sport.

"I want to experiment with songs, be as creative as possible and develop a sound of my own."

Mbinga (second from right) during his time at Ajax

By the age of 17, Mbinga was living the dream of many aspiring footballers in the Netherlands.

After impressing at boyhood club PEC Zwolle, he earned a move to Ajax and began a new life in Amsterdam away from his mother and seven siblings.

During his four seasons at the club, he shared the dressing room with brothers Quinten and Jurrien Timber, now of Crystal Palace and Arsenal, who joined Ajax from Feyenoord around the same time Mbinga arrived from Zwolle.

"We had a feeling that we had joined this journey together," Mbinga recalls. "We stepped in together. Already then, you could see that Quinten and Jurrien were like machines. They were built like machines from a young age."

He remembers the technical elegance of Liverpool midfielder Gravenberch and the physical prowess of striker Brobbey, who went on to score 56 goals in 163 appearances for Ajax's first team before moving to Sunderland last September.

Mbinga also had the opportunity to test himself against some of Europe's biggest clubs, including Real Madrid, Manchester United and Manchester City.

At one point, he even captained the group and saw little to separate them in terms of ability. However, their careers would take very different paths.

"In terms of talent, there wasn't really a big difference at the time," he says.

"Then, maybe two or three years later, Ryan Gravenberch had already made his first-team debut for Ajax. So it's all about development, right? And the same goes for the other guys."

Looking back, Mbinga now deeply treasures those years and the opportunity to have played alongside such talented footballers.

"I played with some amazing, talented players, and at the time, you already knew that they were really talented, right? It's the highest level," he says.

"But you don't know that they're going to become Premier League stars in the upcoming years. So that's amazing to look back at."

After struggling to break through, Mbinga returned to PEC Zwolle in 2021 at the age of 20, where the familiar, less pressurised surroundings prompted him to consider life beyond football and his ambition to build something of his own.

"I think it was also part of the personal growth. I really liked the music. I also liked looking up to the other artists at the time who were popping," Mbinga says.

"For me, it was also a dream to do something in music, create my own songs. But at that time, I was really talented with football, but I couldn't make music yet."

Mbinga made his professional debut for his local side in September 2021, coming off the bench against Ajax, of all teams, in the Eredivisie.

But the youngster would make just five further first-team appearances as Zwolle were relegated, before dropping down the Dutch football pyramid.

He ended up playing semi-professionally in the fourth tier to fund his music career.

"When I made my professional debut, everything went really well. I signed the contract and everything," he says.

"But the purpose of creating something for myself in terms of music, being very creative, was getting stronger."

Five years on, that gamble is paying off. He has almost 500,000 monthly Spotify listeners, while his 2024 track Mentality has surpassed 16 million streams.

Every now and again, making music offers Mbinga a thrill similar to that he once chased on the football pitch.

"For me, all the achievements in music are like I'm scoring a goal or I'm giving an assist or playing a good match," he laughs.

"And of course, if one of my songs really takes off, then it feels like I'm scoring the winning goal in a very important game - like a final!"

AS Monaco and Spain forward Ansu Fati (left) with Elikia Mbinga

Although Mbinga remains content with his decision not to pursue a career in professional football, he remains closely connected to the sport that shaped his life.

Earlier this month, he travelled to the United Kingdom to promote his new album, First of a Kind, allowing him to reunite with former Ajax team-mates Jurrien and Quinten Timber.

Mbinga attended an Arsenal Champions League match at Emirates Stadium and a Premier League Crystal Palace game at Selhurst Park.

"I'm really focused on creating this world for the people, for the fans," says Mbinga. "Creating a world that can unite football and music - like a creative bridge."

Another footballer supporting his musical journey is Spain forward Ansu Fati, who plays for AS Monaco.

The pair met as teenagers at a youth tournament in Europe when Fati was at Barcelona and have remained close friends ever since.

In February, Mbinga released a song dedicated to the forward and the challenges he has faced since breaking through at Barcelona in 2019.

Fati was seen as one of the new generation of La Masia stars at Camp Nou, making 51 appearances for the first team in 2022-23.

But he was loaned to Brighton the following season and struggled for minutes on his return to the Catalan giants, eventually joining Monaco on loan last season in a deal that became permanent in the summer.

Mbinga wrote the track in 2024 but agreed with Fati to release it only when the "time was right".

"You know what's crazy? Seeing him again and seeing everything that he's gone through," he recalls. "We went out to eat, went out for dinner, and then he was playing my song in the car, singing it lyric for lyric.

"I was like, 'wow, this life is crazy, man'."

Mary Peltola defeated the state's Republican incumbent after a controversial race

Democrat Mary Peltola has won Alaska's hard-fought Senate race, completing a sweeping victory for the party in the US upper house in the midterm elections.

The win gives the Democrats a 56th Senate seat following a tumultuous and controversial election in Alaska, which featured alleged spoiler recruitment efforts and unprecedented court battles.

It took two full weeks of counting to call a winner in the 3 November poll due to the logistical challenge of collecting ballots from across the state's remote expanse.

The Democratic win is the ninth Senate seat the party took from Republicans in this year's midterms, giving the party control of the US Congress for the last two years of Donald Trump's presidency.

A historic set of victories nationally also saw the party win back the House of Representatives.

In her victory statement, Peltola said the "status quo in DC is not working for Alaska".

She recalled speaking to "elders in tears about empty fish racks" and to parents in rural Alaska choosing between heating their homes and putting food on the table.

Peltola's campaign had come under fire after the New York Times reported Democrats attempted to recruit a candidate named Daniel J Sullivan, a complete political unknown residing in a small coastal town who shared a name with the state's current US Senator and incumbent, Dan S Sullivan, in an alleged attempt to confuse voters.

Trump says Alaska voters chose the wrong Dan Sullivan. What does the data show?

Could Alaska's fishing industry tilt Washington's balance of power?

After legal challenges, state courts ruled the second Daniel J Sullivan could remain on the ballot, and election officials distinguished them on election materials.

Peltola denied having knowledge of the alleged plot but her campaign swiftly came under fire, and both the justice department and Alaska's Republican governor said they would launch investigations.

The Trump administration then filed a lawsuit attempting to stop the certification of the election results if the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan lost.

A federal judge, though, dismissed the case, following legal challenges from Alaska election officials as well as the Peltola campaign and voting groups.

Due to Alaska's ranked-choice voting system, voters confused about which Dan Sullivan was the incumbent could simply choose each man as their first and second choice.

If they did so, after the first round of voting was complete, tabulation would re-allocate any votes from the non-incumbent Dan Sullivan - who stood little to no chance of winning - to the US Senator.

Experts told the BBC that this process made it difficult for any potential spoiler candidate to have any impact on the results.

An analysis by BBC Verify found that even if every vote for the other Dan Sullivan had gone to the incumbent, Peltola would still have won.

The seat initially was one of several toss-up races that appeared as a must-win for Democrats if they wanted to gain control of the Senate - but by the time Peltola was called the winner, they had seats to spare.

With 99% of ballots counted, Peltola had slightly more than 50%, while Sullivan trailed on less than 46%.

Sullivan, a former Alaska attorney general and an ally of Trump, campaigned on his record of delivering energy and military investment for the state.

Peltola promised Alaskans a more independent voice in Washington.

"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," she said in her victory statement.

"I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska's working families."
