A Pakistani man with ties to Iran's government has been sentenced to 27 years in prison for his role in a plot to assassinate US President Donald Trump and other officials.

Asif Merchant was found guilty in March of attempting to commit an act of terrorism transcending national boundaries and murder for hire after trying to hire hitmen to kill Trump, former President Joe Biden, and former US ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley.

The hitmen were instead undercover FBI agents.

In court, he said he was acting under the direction of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to avenge the 2020 US assassination of Qasem Soleimani, Iran's topmost military commander.

New York US federal judge Eric Ross Komitee sentenced Merchant on Tuesday to 330 months (27 years and six months) in prison, months after a jury handed its guilty verdict.

Although other US officials were potential targets, the assassination plot was largely focused on Trump because he was president at the time Soleimani was killed. Trump has spoken publicly about ordering the US airstrike that killed the Iranian general while he was travelling in Iraq.

In response to the killing, Iran's late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei said "severe revenge awaits the criminals" behind the attack.

Prosecutors said Merchant initially travelled to Iran for religious pilgrimages and he was then introduced to an IRGC handler. He travelled to Iran 15 times where he received training from Iranian intelligence officers, prosecutors said, before flying to the US in April 2024 to carry out the plot.

Prosecutors said Merchant paid $5,000 to the undercover hitmen as part of an initial payment. He was arrested in July 2024 in Texas as he was about to leave the US.

In court, Merchant argued that he "had no other option" than to go along with the plot because his handler indicated that he knew who Merchant's Iranian relatives were and where they lived.

He said he had anticipated being arrested before anyone was killed and intended to cooperate with the US government, CBS, the BBC's US partner reported. He had hoped that would help him obtain a green card.

The jury deliberated for less than two hours before returning its verdict, US media said.

"An Iranian agent who came to the United States to coordinate an assassination attempt against President Trump has been justly sentenced for his criminal conduct," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement.

"The Department of Justice will not tolerate foreign terrorist plots against our leaders and will not stop until those responsible are held accountable."

MN202611_1nmpr0iinhc.t:
The military plane, seen above, was effectively destroyed by the vandalism

US officials have charged an Irishman with destroying a $60m (£45m) American military aircraft after he allegedly sneaked onto the tarmac of an airport in Ireland.

Daithi O'Corrain, 48, is accused of doing extensive research before he allegedly used chemicals and various tools - including an axe - to damage a US Air National Guard C-130 Hercules parked at Shannon Airport near Limerick.

American prosecutors have charged him with destruction of government property, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.

O'Corrain is not currently in US custody, according to the Associated Press news agency, and it is unclear whether he has a lawyer who could speak on his behalf.

In filings unsealed by prosecutors in New York on Tuesday, agents from the FBI argued that the act jeopardised US national security. They say the plane was parked at the airport while en route to another country on a US military assignment.

"As alleged, Daithi O'Corrain carried out a deliberate, planned attack against a US military aircraft, causing tens of millions of dollars in damage and jeopardizing critical military operations," prosecutors said in a court filing.

"This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism," said FBI Assistant Director in Charge James Barnacle Jr, explaining O'Corrain "spent months researching the aircraft, acquiring tools and materials, and preparing to maximize the destruction he could inflict."

Officials say that the suspect planned extensively for the 11 April 2026 raid, and brought tools with him for the demolition, which took place over several hours.

He entered the plane by breaking a locking mechanism, officials say, then used straps to close the doors before covering the windows.

"O'Corrain then proceeded to inflict severe damage to the interior of the Aircraft by, among other things, cutting wire bundles and hydraulic lines within the Aircraft, crimping a liquid oxygen line within the Aircraft, destroying every gauge in the Aircraft's cockpit, and puncturing the Aircraft's air ducts," the US indictment says.

He also used gallium, a substance that can erode aluminum and steel, ball bearings which he poured in the fuel tank, and an axe which he used to puncture the exterior of the plane.

He was caught by airport crew, and filmed standing on top of the plane. He was arrested at the scene, and charged by Ireland's national police with causing criminal damages.

O'Corrain seen standing on the rear of the aircraft in a handout from the US Department of Justice

The US charges say that he had planned well, because he avoided cutting a line that would have risked causing massive explosion.

According to the Limerick Post , external , O'Corrain is from Cork City. Supporters have described him as an anti-war activist.

Shannon Airport is a key hub for US military personnel, and is frequently the scene of anti-war protests. It was used by President Donald Trump in September for his visit to Ireland.

US prosecutors note that there have been several breaches there in recent years by protesters, including in May 2025 when three people drove a van through a perimeter fence , and then again later that month when a US airplane was sprayed with paint, making it temporarily inoperable.

MN202611_6f9yexykrb.t:
Rassie Erasmus took the South Africa job after the departure of Allister Coetzee

While Rassie Erasmus has run low of advocates elsewhere, in his homeland they rushed to his defence.

"Rassie was just asking questions," said former South Africa hooker Hanyani Shimange in the wake of Erasmus' six-match ban for a scattergun series of complaints about the injustices suffered by his Springboks side.

"But you have to look at the facts. Where was the accountability for that refereeing performance?"

Naas Botha, legendary South Africa fly-half turned pundit, described Erasmus' punishment as a "debacle". "You can't tell me they [officials] are untouchable," he said.

Supersport, which broadcasts South Africa's games domestically, published an article accusing Erasmus' critics of "pearl clutching" , external and "shooting the messenger" with regards to the game's faults.

Despite slurring the officials with a suggestion of match-fixing, Erasmus has the support of South Africa.

His feats with the team are astonishing.

South Africa were ranked sixth in the world when he took over in March 2018.

He arrived off the back of a November tour in which they lost to Wales and were thrashed 38-3 by Ireland. New Zealand had racked up a record 57-0 win a few months earlier.

Erasmus turned the team around at speed, marrying their trademark up-front power with pace out wide.

They won the 2019 World Cup. The defended their title in 2023. They will go into the tournament in 2027 aiming for an unprecedented three-peat. And few would bet against them achieving it.

Long before the sport's data revolution, he was coding game footage, picking up the technique from a friend who worked in the military. He has since developed Outfox, his own software which allows his teams to run through moves virtually on a screen away from the pitch.

Tactically, he has also been ahead of the curve. He pioneered the use of forward-heavy replacement benches, giving his team an edge in the final quarter of the match. He saw the game-breaking potential of diminutive Sevens specialist Kurt-Lee Arendse and moulded Andre Esterhuizen into a genuine hybrid player, capable of playing in the back row and the backline.

Trick plays - forcing a scrum with a deliberate infringement off kick-off, or setting up a line-out in the middle of the pitch - have been part of Erasmus' arsenal.

Legally, he is across every possible loophole.

There was controversy before the match against France last weekend when he made use of the Nations Championships looser regulations to swap his starting front row just over an hour before kick-off. Previously, he demoted himself to water boy so he could run the touchline during the 2021 series win over the British and Irish Lions.

Former Springbok wing Brian Habana worked under Erasmus at the Stormers in Cape Town.

"He is one of the master tacticians the game has ever seen," Habana told BBC Sport's Ireland Rugby Social.

"I don't always agree with how Rassie comes across, but I understand he wears his heart on his sleeve. He has got incredibly high standards.

"He's willing to be in the firing line to defend what he believes is right."

France's win over South Africa was only the Springboks' third defeat in 11 matches this year

But there is no doubt, by the letter of the law, that Erasmus is wrong - certainly in terms of the platform and terms he chose for his complaints.

In July World Rugby introduced new rules around criticism of officials. It specifically targeted "comments which, viewed objectively, a reasonable person would conclude were an attack on the credibility or competence of the match officials".

Mentioning "match-fixing" undermines the officials in exactly that way.

Considering Erasmus' previous, including an hour-long monologue bemoaning officiating of a first-Test defeat by the Lions in 2021 and a series of tweets after a loss to France a year later, he may be fortunate to only be banned for six matches.

World Rugby, perhaps pre-empting the reaction in South Africa, was clear that it was not punishing Erasmus for asking questions.

"Robust, respectful debate is natural, but teams have access to well-established and supported channels and protocols for raising officiating matters before and after matches," it said in its judgement.

"Challenging a decision is not the same as questioning an official's integrity or making comments that expose them to personal abuse."

For many South Africans, though, Erasmus is still an outlaw hero.

World Rugby, based in Dublin, is seen by them as tilted towards the north.

Australian Brett Robinson, the current chairman, is the first figure from outside the Six Nations countries to hold the organisation's top job since it became an elected position.

The World Cup has been lifted by South Africa on four occasions, but held there only once.

Japan coach Eddie Jones, Erasmus' fellow maverick, recently suggested Ireland's political clout , external was behind his team's home game being staged in Australia rather than Tokyo.

South Africa were a powerful voice against the possible moves to "depower" the scrum - a key part of the Springbok game - at a February conference to discuss future law tweaks.

Erasmus' public pronouncements have fuelled conspiracy theories weaved from those threads. They have also made an all-time great team harder for outsiders to love.

Whether it is a deliberate ploy is hard to tell.

Certainly Erasmus is a repeat offender, but his offences have also come in his second language. He is an Afrikaans speaker.

Some also see instinctive honesty rather than premeditated ploy in his public speaking.

"He also has almost no filters, so he will speak his mind without fully appreciating the consequences of what he has done," his biographer David O'Sullivan told BBC Sport in 2023.

Whatever the motivation, the consequences keep coming - for Erasmus, but also the rest of world rugby.

Referees Nic Berry and Wayne Barnes, previous targets of Erasmus' criticism, have detailed the effects it had on them.

Berry described "a character assassination" that caused "immeasurable damage". He has not refereed a South Africa game in the five years since.

Barnes' wife and children were threatened over social media.

South Africa's latest appeal to their supporters not to abuse officials , external may be too late for referee Andrea Piardi and his television match official Matteo Liperini, who oversaw France's win on Friday.

For a complex sport, the image of a world champion coach publicly criticising officials does not little to dispel a wavering viewer's assumption that it is too intricate and confusing to justify their attention.

South Africa will always line up alongside their rebel chief.

But the patience of the rest of the rugby world with Erasmus' antics is wearing ever thinner.

The Prince and Princess of Wales have met Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi as part of their three-day visit to India.

William and Catherine arrived in New Dehli on Wednesday for the final leg of their first official oversees trip together in four years.

The meeting was a late addition to the couple's schedule and came after Modi confirmed he would be back from a scheduled trip to the Philippines in time to see the royals.

It comes a day after the royal couple were in Mumbai for the annual Earthshot Prize, which was founded by the prince and remains one of his biggest personal projects.

Street cricket with a legend then metro ride as William and Kate begin India visit

When he announced earlier this year that it was going to be held in India for the first time, the prince highlighted India's leadership in climate innovation, its biodiversity and its massive youth population as the key reasons for choosing the country.

A Kensington Palace spokesperson said ahead of the Modi meeting: "For the Prince, it represents another significant engagement as he continues to take on a growing role on the international stage,

"We've seen him increasingly support the UK's diplomatic relationships through his overseas engagements, and this meeting will provide an opportunity to build on those connections at the highest level."

The couple last met Modi on their official visit to India in 2016.

On Tuesday the prince and princess were in Mumbai to announce the winners of the annual Earthshot Prize.

The event, founded by Prince William in 2020, was hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.

Five separate winners were named during Tuesday's ceremony and each will receive £1m to scale up their projects.

Speaking at the ceremony, Prince William said the 2020s were the time when positive change becomes "irreversible", adding history was "not written by challenges alone", but also by those who rose to meet them.

The princess presented on the five awards and, as she did so, said the entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists tackling the environmental crisis brought her "hope".

Rwanda has called for greater African representation and leadership in international initiatives aimed at advancing the rights and opportunities of women and girls, arguing that the continent should be treated as an equal partner in shaping development priorities rather than merely a recipient of support.

The call was made by Rwanda’s Ambassador to Denmark and other Nordic countries, Diane Gashumba, during the Copenhagen Day of Action: From Declaration to Delivery, held on November 17, 2026.

The meeting, organised by the Nordic Council of Ministers in partnership with the Gates Foundation, brought together international leaders and development partners to discuss how commitments on gender equality and women’s empowerment can be translated into practical action.

Gashumba participated in the closing panel discussion, titled ‘What Collective Action Looks Like,” alongside South Africa’s Minister Sindisiwe Chikunga, Mexican Ambassador Norma Bertha Pensado Moreno, Gates Foundation representative Joe Cerrell and Karen Ellemann of the Nordic Council of Ministers.

During the discussion, the Rwandan diplomat highlighted the country’s progress in investing in women and girls, particularly through the use of emerging technologies to improve maternal and child health and reduce preventable deaths.

She emphasised that African countries must have a stronger voice in determining the direction of global development programmes, noting that their participation should go beyond receiving financial and technical assistance.

“African countries should not be seen merely as beneficiaries of global initiatives, but as partners and leaders in shaping the programmes and decisions that affect their people,”was the central message of her intervention.

She also pointed to the Africa-Nordic Health Summit as an important platform for strengthening cooperation between African and Nordic countries, particularly in advancing healthcare priorities and creating opportunities for shared learning and investment.

The summit is expected to provide greater space for African perspectives, leadership and priorities in international health discussions, while encouraging stronger partnerships between the two regions.

The Copenhagen Day of Action was organised as a follow-up to commitments made at the Copenhagen conference on gender equality and the rights of women and girls, with a focus on moving beyond declarations and political promises towards measurable results.

The discussions reflect growing calls for international development partnerships to place greater emphasis on local leadership, accountability and practical interventions that improve the lives of women and girls.

Uganda Airlines has officially launched daily direct flights between Kigali and Entebbe, marking a significant development in air connectivity between the neighboring countries and opening new opportunities for trade, tourism, investment and international travel.

The service commenced on November 18, 2026, establishing a direct connection between Kigali International Airport and Entebbe International Airport and offering passengers greater convenience when travelling between the two East African destinations.

Speaking at the launch ceremony in Kigali, Rwanda’s Minister of State, Col. Claudien Bizimungu, welcomed the development, describing improved air connectivity as an important driver of economic cooperation and regional integration.

Bizimungu said the daily flights would make movement between the two countries easier, allowing people to travel more conveniently while creating opportunities for businesses, investors and tourism operators.

He emphasised that stronger air links would facilitate the movement of people, goods and services, while supporting cross-border trade and expanding economic partnerships.

The minister also highlighted the importance of continued investment in aviation infrastructure, operational efficiency and service delivery to strengthen the country’s position as a regional transport and business hub.

Uganda Airlines Chief Executive Officer Girma Wake described Kigali as a natural addition to the carrier’s regional network, citing the longstanding economic, social and cultural relationships between the two countries.

“The Kigali-Entebbe route has been long overdue, given the close economic, social and cultural ties between our two countries. Kigali is a natural fit,” Wake said.

He added that the service would also connect passengers departing from Kigali to the airline’s wider international network through Entebbe, providing access to destinations across Africa, the Middle East, Asia and Europe.

For travelers, the connection offers an additional option for accessing international destinations without necessarily routing their journeys through other regional aviation hubs.

The daily service is expected to benefit business travelers, tourists, government officials, conference participants and people visiting family and friends. It could also encourage more tourism exchanges by making it easier for visitors to combine destinations in both countries.

Beyond passenger transportation, improved connectivity is expected to support commercial activities by facilitating business meetings, investment engagements and the movement of professionals between the two markets.

With the addition of Kigali, Uganda Airlines has expanded its network to 18 destinations, following the introduction of flights to Accra, Ghana, on October 27, 2026.

The development forms part of the carrier’s wider expansion strategy, which seeks to strengthen its regional presence while connecting Uganda to more international markets.

Uganda Airlines, the country’s national carrier, was revived in 2018, seven years after the original airline was liquidated in 2001. It resumed commercial operations in August 2019, restoring Uganda’s national air transport services after an 18-year absence.

The launch of the Kigali–Entebbe service comes amid broader efforts to deepen economic cooperation and regional integration within East Africa, where efficient air transport remains essential for business mobility, tourism and cross-border commercial activities.

As economic relations between the neighboring countries continue to evolve, the new daily connection is expected to provide another platform for strengthening people-to-people ties and unlocking opportunities across the region.

The mother of a four-year-old girl killed in central France and found along a motorway almost 40 years ago has been sentenced to 20 years in prison.

Halima El Bakhti, 72, was found guilty on Tuesday of "torture and acts of barbarity resulting in death without the intent to kill", French media reports.

The girl's father, 74-year-old Ahmed Touloub, was handed a 15-year sentence as an accomplice.

Four-year-old Inass Touloub was found along the A10 road in Suèvres in the Loir-et-Cher department on 11 August 1987. Her body bore multiple marks of abuse, including human bite marks, broken bones and burns with an iron.

She was buried in an unmarked grave near the location where her body was found. Unidentified for three decades, she was known only as the "Little Martyr of the A10".

Then, in 2018, she was identified after the DNA of her brother – tested in an unrelated case – matched with hers, leading to the arrest of their parents.

The trial took place in Loir-et-Cher Assize Court from 2 November, with the verdict delivered on Tuesday after several hours of deliberation.

During the trial, prosecutor Anaïs Allio emphasised that "not a single part of Inass's body was spared", and recalled the "sense of vertigo that overcame us all" upon viewing the "unbearable photographs" from the autopsy, France Info reports.

The jury concluded that the child's mother was suffering from impaired judgement at the time of the girl's death, which reduced the maximum potential sentence.

The couple have 10 days to appeal the verdict.

Inass's death sparked one of France's biggest ever investigations, with the girl's photograph posted in public places and an alert sent to more than 30 countries.

Jeffries was re-elected as the party leader in a closed-door vote on Wednesday. He has served as minority leader since 2023.

Is it too early for the Premier League bottom three to worry?

Despite being only 10 games into the season, sitting in the relegation zone even at this early stage is more worrying than you might think.

But with how tight the Premier League table is, this could also be one of the fiercest relegation battles we have seen in a long time.

Two of the current bottom three, Crystal Palace and Manchester United , will resume their campaigns at the weekend with new managers after appointing Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino respectively.

Sunderland , sandwiching the pair in 19th, have not pressed the panic button and have kept faith with Regis le Bris.

But is it too early to worry? We look at what the stats tell us about about relegation battles in the past and what we can learn for the months ahead.

Looking at every Premier League season since it changed to a 20-team league in 1995-96, the current bottom three have cause to be concerned.

In 19 of the previous 31 seasons (61%), only one of the bottom three sides after 10 games managed to avoid relegation.

For fairness and accuracy, the 'bottom three' are the three sides with the worst record after 10 games, not simply those in the relegation zone after matchweek 10, since in some seasons a team had played nine games by that point.

Only in 10 seasons (32%) have two or more of the bottom three stayed up - and that has not happened in any of the past eight campaigns. The last time more than one team avoided the drop was in 2017-18, when all three survived.

That has only happened twice, although only twice have all three sides been relegated.

Overall, of the 93 previous teams in the bottom three after 10 games, 41 survived and 52 were relegated - a survival rate of 44%.

This is the third time that Palace have been bottom after 10 games. On both previous occasions, they did not just survive but thrived, finishing 11th.

They did so under Tony Pulis in 2013-14 and under Roy Hodgson in 2017-18. Both managers, like Frank, were appointed early in the season following poor starts under Ian Holloway and Frank de Boer respectively.

The 2013-14 season is the only previous time that Sunderland and Palace were the bottom two at this stage. The Black Cats also survived thanks to a great, late escape under Gus Poyet.

This is the first time United have been in the bottom three after 10 games of a Premier League season.

Given the size and resources of the club, it is unlikely they will go down, although the team in 18th place at this stage have been relegated in each of the past six seasons.

Fans of all three clubs will hope for a repeat of 2017-18, when not only Palace but the bottom three improved significantly to finish comfortably mid-table.

While history suggests only one of the bottom three will survive, there is also evidence to suggest that this might not be a standard Premier League season.

Palace have seven points, which is the most the bottom side after 10 games have had for 24 years. The bottom three all had eight points in 2002-03.

Sunderland 's eight points is also the most the side in 19th place have had for 16 years. Wolves had nine points in 2010-11 and survived in 17th.

In fact, only five points separate the bottom half of the Premier League, with Tottenham in 11th on 12 points and Palace bottom with seven – the smallest gap at this stage for 24 years.

The highest that a team in the bottom three after 10 games have finished the season is eighth - Bolton in 2003-04, Tottenham in 2008-09 and Everton in 2017-18 - which suggests it will be Conference League at best for United next season.

Then again, the table is so tight that only nine points separate Chelsea in fifth and Palace - the smallest gap at this stage for 16 years.

Given that fifth place has been enough to qualify for the Champions League in recent seasons, optimistic United fans may not be ruling it out just yet.

That means even sides who have started well could be involved in the relegation battle.

The most points a team have had after 10 games of a 38-game season and been relegated is 14 - Joe Royle's Manchester City in 2000-01.

The most recent team to start well but be relegated were Eddie Howe's Bournemouth in 2019-20, who were sitting pretty in ninth with 13 points at this stage but went down on the final day.

As mentioned, this season has both the 'best' bottom side in terms of points and the most compact bottom half of the table that we have seen at this stage since 2002-03.

That season West Ham were relegated on the final day with 42 points - the most a side have been relegated with in Premier League history.

Given the way this season is shaping up, 40 points might also not be enough to survive.

Dáithí Mac Gabhann walked out with Republic of Ireland's Troy Parrott as Ireland won 3-0 over Kosovo in the Nations League

A 10-year-old boy who inspired changes to Northern Ireland's organ donation laws "skipped" onto the pitch as a mascot at the Republic of Ireland match on Tuesday evening.

It was "the best night of his life" and is something he would not have been able to do without the gift of a new heart, his father Máirtín said.

Dáithí Mac Gabhann received a transplant in July after an eight-year wait, and his father said he is "doing incredible" and "living his life to the absolute fullest".

Dáithí walked out with Republic of Ireland's Troy Parrott as Ireland won 3-0 over Kosovo in the Nations League , with Parrott having scored two of the goals.

It wasn't the first time Dáithí has been a mascot. A couple of years ago he walked out with Toni Leigh Finnegan for the Women's Irish Cup final with Cliftonville and Glentoran.

However, Finnegan had to carry him out as he required a wheelchair at the time.

Máirtín said Dáithí skipped out with Troy Parrott and "wasn't out of breath once", something that would not have been possible before his transplant

"He had such an amazing experience, but this time he skipped out, and he skipped out simply because of the gift of organ donation, and how incredible the gift of organ donation is," Máirtín told BBC News NI.

"So he skipped out with Troy Parrott, wasn't out of breath once, sang as loud as he could, and was just absolutely full of beans the whole night, and he no way, not a chance, would he have been able to walk out that far had he not received the gift of a heart transplant."

Máirtín said his experience has "created a bit of a monster" as on Wednesday morning Dáithí was "outright refusing" to wear his uniform to school or wash his hands, as Troy Parrott had held them.

"So he's away into school with unwashed hands and in his Ireland kit from last night and I've never been happier for him to put his foot down and say, 'I'm not wearing a uniform today'."

Dáithí was so excited after his experience at the match that he went to school on Wednesday in his full Ireland kit

Dáithí was born in 2016 with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, meaning that side of his heart did not form correctly.

In 2023 a law was introduced in Northern Ireland which means that people automatically become potential organ donors unless they explicitly say they wish not to be.

The legislation - officially the Organ and Tissue Donation (Deemed Consent) Act (Northern Ireland) 2022 - was known as Dáithí's Law, after his family spent years campaigning on the issue.

Dáithí Mac Gabhann received a heart transplant in July after an eight year wait

Last week, Dáithí was "screaming down the phone" when he received the call from players Chiedozie "Chieo" Ogbene, Caoimhín Kelleher and Troy Parrott asking him to be a mascot , external .

His many years of campaigning for a change to organ donation laws first caught the attention of the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) when he was two-years-old.

However, the journey down to Dublin for the match on Tuesday wasn't smooth sailing as the Dublin Port Tunnel was closed and the family were worried they would miss the start.

So much was the scurry that Máirtín had to stay behind for the initial walk out onto the pitch and Dáithí's grandad brought him in.

"I have never been so happy to have missed Dáithí walking out in front of 50,000 people with Troy Parrott, because it meant he made it," he said.

"I was screaming in the car when I saw the photo because I was just so happy, I obviously would have loved to have been there, but it didn't matter anymore, it was as if Ireland scored the winner in the 90th minute.

"But I also said to Dáithí this is a lesson to you - why you never ever give up, because we shouldn't have made it in time, I just said we're not giving up here, so we're going to keep trying."

Watch: Fiona the hippo under observation after eating hat

The Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio says its beloved hippopotamus Fiona is undergoing emergency medical care after swallowing a knit hat that slipped into her enclosure.

The Zoo said that Fiona had swallowed the hat about nine days ago and was asymptomatic at first, adding that she was "large enough that a small-ish hat should be passing through".

But a few days later, her appetite started to decrease, and the zoo staff were trying to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system.

Fiona rose to fame when she was born premature at the Cincinnati Zoo and at first struggled to survive. Her story inspired an ice cream flavour as well as a character in Cincinnati's ballet.

Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, told US media that the hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.

"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.

Zoo staff have been providing a series of supportive measures like fluids and ultrasounds to help Fiona recover.

The latest ultrasound showed the hat passing through Fiona's small intestine, the staff said, adding that she is still a bit dehydrated.

"Surgery isn't an option for full-grown hippos and our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she could pass this on her own," one of the zookeepers said in an update.

Fiona was born six weeks early to 17-year-old hippo Bibi on 24 January.

At birth she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species.

The zoo said staff were "rooting for her and hoping that she proves to be as strong and resilient as she was at the beginning of her life".

Danika Priim denies one count of sexual assault

A former England rugby league player and TV pundit accused of putting her hand up a woman's skirt in a cricket club toilet has told a jury it "categorically did not happen".

Danika Priim, 42, has been charged with carrying out the alleged sexual assault in the toilets at Horsforth Cricket Club in Leeds on 22 July 2022.

Her accuser, who cannot be named for legal reasons, previously told a trial at Leeds Crown Court how Priim twice reached up her dress and grabbed her underwear.

Keighley-based Priim, who previously represented Bradford Bulls, Leeds Rhinos and England, including at the 2017 World Cup, denies one count of sexual assault. The trial continues.

Two of the complainant's friends told the court they also witnessed what happened in the toilet but, on Wednesday, Priim told the jury she was never in the toilets with the three women.

Prosecutor Chloe Hudson put it to Priim that there were only two alternatives – either she was lying or the complainant and her two friends were lying.

Priim told the jury: "It categorically did not happen."

The defendant agreed she was not suggesting that it was an accident, or the woman had invited her to touch her, or it was a joke.

Priim told the jury she was never in the toilets with the complainant, adding: "I did not touch (her) in the toilets at all."

Hudson said to her: "What you must be saying is that these three got together to make completely false allegations about you."

Priim responded: "It's the biggest question I have – it's the why."

The prosecutor asked the defendant about how the complainant demonstrated to the jury how she was grabbed.

Priim said: "She was lying. I did not do that."

She added: "I'm also a very happy heterosexual woman. I'm with a man. I live with a man."

The prosecutor said: "The truth is that you sexually assaulted (the woman), didn't you?"

Priim said: "The truth is that it never happened."

Danika Priim, right, represented England at the 2017 World Cup

Hudson asked Priim whether she thought the complainant and her two friends had colluded in a "witch hunt against you".

Stood in the witness box wearing a chunky light brown cardigan and a cream-and-black scarf, Priim replied: "I believe they have."

On Tuesday, the complainant described how Priim "walked straight up to me and put her hand up my skirt and grabbed hold of my pants and my private parts".

The woman said she asked the defendant what she was doing, "then she did it again, grinning at me, and walked off".

One of the complainant's friends told the jury how she witnessed Priim put her hand up the woman's skirt.

She told the court: "I recall seeing her remove her hand, laughed about it and then repeated it.

Giving evidence on Wednesday, Priim said she only went to the toilet once during her time at the cricket club, and produced a photograph she took of her and two friends in there, to help the jury with timings.

She said she drove to the venue and was drinking soft drinks until later when she had one pint.

Asked about the police getting involved following the allegation, she said: "It absolutely broke me."

Since retiring from the game in 2021 Priim has appeared on BBC, Channel 4 and Sky Sports as a pundit, reporter and commentator.

Jurors were sent out to consider their verdict on Wednesday.

Singer Julio Iglesias is facing an investigation by Spain's national court over allegations he sexually abused and assaulted two female former staff members

Two women, who worked for the 83-year-old in the Caribbean, have accused him of abuse which they say took place in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic in 2021.

The announcement comes after Spanish prosecutors dropped an inquiry into the claims earlier this year after concluding that they lacked jurisdiction because the alleged crimes took place abroad.

Iglesias, who has been a household name in Spain since the 1960s and has sold millions of records worldwide, has previously denied the allegations .

But in a statement published on Wednesday , external (in Spanish), national court Judge Antonio Piña said the account given in the complaint, alongside preliminary evidence provided, justified opening criminal proceedings.

He added that the investigation would cover parts of the complaint relating to potential crimes against sexual freedom, as well as assault and degrading treatment.

But the court will not investigate claims made in the lawsuit of human trafficking or crimes against workers' rights. Piña said these allegations were dismissed after the he looked into the hiring of the women and found there was "no deception or artifice involved".

Piña said the former employees had been summoned to testify in person on 3 February.

The announcement comes after Spain's public prosecutor's office shifted its position last month, saying it now believed the court had jurisdiction to investigate the allegations.

In its statement, the national court said Spanish law sets out that courts can hear cases of crimes committed abroad by Spanish citizens provided certain conditions are met.

The allegations against Iglesias first emerged in a joint three-year investigation between Spanish newspaper El Diario , external and television network Univision news, published in January.

In that investigation, the two women were identified as a domestic worker and a physical therapist, who described alleged sexual abuse and degrading working conditions.

The domestic worker, whose name was changed to Rebeca in the reports, said Iglesias would regularly call her to his room at the end of the day and would touch her inappropriately without consent.

Rebeca, a Dominican who was 22 when the alleged events took place, also alleged that Iglesias had forced her to take part in threesomes with another female member of staff. She also described the singer slapping her in the face and grabbing her genitals.

The other woman, a Venezuelan physical therapist named as Laura in the article, said Iglesias had touched her breasts and kissed her on the mouth against her will. She added that he constantly threatened to fire her, controlled how much food she ate and asked her about when her period was due.

Rebeca and Laura filed an initial legal complaint in January against Iglesias for sexual assault and human trafficking.

In a response to the allegations in January, Iglesias said , external : "I deny having abused, coerced, or disrespected any woman. These accusations are absolutely false and deeply sadden me."

On Wednesday, the court said the lawsuit had been accepted based on evidence provided in the complaint. This included a photograph of one of the complainants, showing a bruise on her arm that was "consistent with the possibility of her being grabbed forcefully".

It added that the same photo showed "two marks on one of her thighs that could correspond to a human bite", which the complainant said were "a consequence of her forced participation in acts of a sexual nature".

WhatsApp message exchanges, including New Year's greetings, which suggest an "affectionate" relationship between the women and Iglesias, will also be considered, the court said.

But it added that the seemingly cordial tone, which presents "an apparent discrepancy with certain aspects of the narrative", would be clarified through a "complete and contextualised examination of the communications".

The claim over violations of workers' rights could not be investigated because there is no comparable criminal offence in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic, where the alleged crimes took place, it said.

Iglesias is one of the most successful Latin artists of all time, having sold more than 300 million records in a career spanning decades.

He is also the father of fellow music superstar Enrique Iglesias.

James McPake may not have given up on football management but the former Dundee and Dunfermline Athletic boss is discovering there is life beyond the dugout.

Four months after moving to Dubai with his family, the 41-year-old has settled into a new role working in schools to develop young players.

It is a considerable change from the pressures of Scottish football but one that McPake and his family had been contemplating for more than a year.

His wife Dawn, a teacher, secured a position in Dubai before McPake landed his own opportunity, one that has opened up a different world of opportunities, including working alongside some recognisable names in football.

"It's certainly a bit different from back home but we're enjoying it," said McPake, who won an international cap with Northern Ireland in 2012.

"There is obviously a big demand for British curriculum teachers, so Dawn managed to get a position and I've been pretty fortunate to land here."

The timing of the family's move has inevitably attracted attention, given the wider tensions in the Middle East and concerns about security in the region.

However, McPake insists their experience of living in Dubai has been very different from some of the headlines.

"You don't hear a lot about it and you don't see anything. It is very much business as usual," he explains. "It's as busy as when we've come here on holiday. It's just like being anywhere else.

"The girls are enjoying it. They feel safe, they enjoy school and they can go out and play at night. We've had no issues that I've seen."

McPake's decision to head overseas has also provided an opportunity to step away from the demands of management and concentrate on developing players.

His responsibilities include overseeing under-16 and under-19 programmes at an impressive set-up, with school timetables adapted to accommodate training and facilities including strength and conditioning rooms, pools and pitches.

"The programme is relatively new but it's similar to the way you would look at an SFA performance school," he says. "The facilities are fantastic. It's difficult not to make a difference when you have facilities like these."

Former Real Madrid and Wales star Gareth Bale recently spent time at the school, answering questions from senior pupils during an hour-long session. And ex- England midfielder Jonjo Shelvey is also working full-time with McPake.

"For the kids, it was a fantastic experience," the former Livingston and Hibernian defender says.

"Gareth sat with myself and the head director of sport and answered question after question. Afterwards, we saw him out on the pitch with some of the younger kids, and Jonjo was on one of our other pitches.

"It's brilliant for the youngsters to have that sort of access to people who have played at the highest level."

McPake's departure from Scotland came at a time when opportunities were becoming increasingly difficult to secure. He admits that was a consideration in the move but not the driving force behind the family's decision.

There remains an obvious desire to return to the dugout but for now he is happy to embrace a different challenge.

"We've always wanted to give this a go, particularly for the girls. We wanted them to have an experience of a different society and culture and broaden their eyes to the world while they were still young," he says.

"The lack of opportunities in Scotland didn't make the decision for us but it certainly didn't cause us any hesitation when we were looking at coming out here.

"We've now been here for a few months, we're settled and we're used to life out here. It's been excellent and better than we imagined."

Although he is now thousands of miles away, McPake continues to follow Scottish football closely, particularly the fortunes of two clubs where he managed.

Dundee, where he was in charge between 2019 and 2022, have impressed him under Steven Pressley. And he also retains an affection for Dunfermline, where he won the League 1 title.

There is particular pride in watching youngsters he helped introduce to senior football begin to make their mark at a higher level.

"Luke Graham getting his first start for Scotland the other night was fantastic. He's a great kid and, even when he was really young and training with us at Dundee, you could see he was going to be the next one," says McPake, who played once for Northern Ireland.

McPake also keeps an eye on the progress of Dunfermline's Tod brothers, Andrew and Jon, who have both progressed through the Scotland international age groups.

There is also no lingering resentment towards either Dundee or Dunfermline, despite the manner in which his managerial spells ended.

McPake acknowledges that losing a job hurts but insists the affection he has for both clubs remains.

"At Dundee, it was excellent," he adds. "I have no bitterness towards them and Dunfermline is the same. We felt we weren't quite backed there.

"Should we have done better? Yes. But we won a very strong League 1 and then they just didn't push on in the Championship."

Congressmen Joe Wilson and Ryan Zinke, and Senator Mike Rounds

Three American lawmakers have called on President Donald Trump’s administration to reconsider sanctions against Rwanda. They say the measures risk undermining the peace agreement between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

The intervention is politically significant. All three lawmakers are Republicans, the party to which Trump belongs. Their position adds a voice from within the President’s own party to criticism of the administration’s approach, which has also come from Democrats.

The Democrats have just secured control of both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections. Their growing influence is expected to bring closer scrutiny of Trump’s foreign policy.

In a letter dated November 16, the lawmakers wrote to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. They criticised sanctions targeting the Rwanda Defence Force (RDF) and Rwanda’s Ministry of Defence.

They argued that the measures were putting pressure on one party while leaving the other with little incentive to honour the agreement.

The letter was signed by Congressmen Joe Wilson and Ryan Zinke, and Senator Mike Rounds.

The lawmakers praised Trump’s efforts to secure peace between Rwanda and the DRC. They described the December 4, 2025 signing of the Washington Accords for Peace and Prosperity as a major diplomatic achievement.

They said the agreement created an opportunity to improve regional security, expand economic cooperation and protect American strategic interests in Central Africa.

But they warned that lasting peace would depend on both governments fulfilling their commitments.

“Recent measures, including Treasury Department sanctions targeting the Rwanda Defense Force and Rwanda’s Ministry of Defense, are handicapping one party, while leaving the other party to the agreement emboldened to pursue a military solution rather than implement the peace agreement,” they wrote.

The lawmakers singled out the need for the DRC to neutralise the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR).

They described the group as an armed organisation with origins in forces responsible for the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi.

Addressing the FDLR threat, they said, remains essential to implementing the Washington Accords and achieving lasting peace.

The letter also acknowledged Rwanda’s stated commitment to the peace process. This includes its readiness to disengage its forces in coordination with the DRC’s implementation of corresponding security commitments.

The lawmakers said Rwanda had continued taking part in joint security discussions. They stressed that both countries’ legitimate security concerns must be addressed.

Their intervention comes amid growing criticism from former American officials over what they see as an uneven approach by the Trump administration.

Tibor Nagy, a former US Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs, has questioned why Washington is sanctioning Rwanda while giving less attention to armed groups he says threaten Rwanda and are supported by the Congolese government. He has argued that targeting only one side will not end the conflict.

Cameron Hudson, a former senior State Department and National Security Council official on Africa, has raised concerns about the administration’s growing focus on Congo’s mineral wealth.

In comments to French newspaper Le Monde, Hudson argued that access to minerals had become the central strategic interest driving US policy in the DRC. His remarks reflect wider concerns that Washington’s pursuit of economic and mineral interests could overshadow the political and security issues behind the conflict.

The three lawmakers called for an approach that gives equal consideration to the commitments and progress of both governments. They said this would preserve diplomatic momentum, strengthen prospects for peace and protect American interests.

The letter comes amid continuing tensions over the implementation of the Washington Accords. Security commitments and the FDLR threat remain major points of disagreement between Kigali and Kinshasa.

The lawmakers thanked Trump for his leadership and pledged support for his administration’s efforts to secure lasting peace in the Great Lakes region.

MN202611_18kvdntoa4n.t:
Watch: Inside the gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war with Russia

There's a new front in the war in Ukraine, and it is underground.

For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.

With a diameter of just over a metre there is enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line – and make it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.

Going underground is now the "only option", says Zanuda, who has helped plan Ukraine's tunnel operation and calls it a new world of fighting. But, he acknowledges, it is hard.

"On the surface you always have some room to manoeuvre, but here you can only engage the enemy head-on."

The journey to get to this subterranean battleground in the Kharkiv region only reinforced the dangers on the ground: a high-speed move by vehicle across open fields, followed by a long march across muddy ground – accompanied by Ukrainian troops with their weapons loaded, ready to shoot down Russian drones.

Arriving at the tunnel entrance, the first thing to hit you is the lingering smell of gas and fetid air.

Both sides use openings in the pipeline to get to the surface, where most of the fighting takes place. They have made breaches in the ground, and used welding tools to break through the thick steel.

The Russians were the first to exploit the pipe to infiltrate the nearby city of Kupyansk in September 2025. They have used underground pipelines before, during the capture of the city of Avdiivka in 2024, and last year in their bid to recapture areas of Russia's Kursk region.

But Ukrainian forces have slowly turned the tables.

Troops move through the tunnel on special sleds - they call it the Kupyansk metro

A specially designed electric cart transports troops and supplies through the pipeline.

They call it the Kupyansk metro. It occasionally breaks down. We travelled on it for 40 minutes, heads bowed and legs crossed. There is a regular bump as you cross the welded sections of the pipe. It is like an austere fairground ride, without the fun.

Our destination was a break in the pipeline where Ukrainian troops have built dug-outs to store ammunition and equipment, with just enough room to stand. It is where the man they call Musician conducts the movement of troops and supplies. He has been living like a mole, his face engrained with dirt and earth.

Musician tells me he has spent the past three months there, with a few brief visits above ground to clean up or go to the toilet. From time to time we can hear the thuds of artillery rounds above. Musician tells me we are close to the line of contact: "But it's safe underground."

Ukrainian troops like Musician rarely see the sun - but they say they feel safer underground

The cart continues its journey into the bowels of the earth. It returns about half an hour later with more troops covered in dirt. They have been fighting in positions on the surface.

There is a look of relief on their dust-caked faces.

"It's more comfortable in the pipe because drones don't fly here, and neither do artillery shells or glide bombs," says Vovochka, who has been fighting on the ground for the past three weeks.

But there has been fighting in the pipeline, too. Operation Veles, named after a mythical Slavic god of the underworld, began in April. Since then Ukraine has advanced 15km (9.3 miles) along the pipeline.

It has been painstaking, backbreaking work – with the ever-present fear of coming into contact with the enemy.

Back above ground we meet a few of the soldiers, from the 13th Khartiia Brigade of Ukraine's National Guard, who have taken part in the mission. Their first task was to clear the detritus, water and Russian barricades inside the pipeline.

The Ukrainian troops say some of the barriers were boobytrapped or piled with Russian bodies. "When we moved them or climbed over them, we had no idea what was underneath," says Chyzh.

The other danger, he said, was the ricochets from gunfire when they tried to advance. "You never know where a bullet is going to go or how it will bounce."

His comrade Kort says "we were all firing, we were pushing them back". Over the course of the operation Ukraine says it killed more than 100 Russian soldiers and took 30 prisoners. "Yes, there were bodies," says Kort. "I even had to sleep right next to them."

The men live and fight in very tight quarters - but have managed to clear 15km of the pipe

Their commander's former life as a miner helped prepare them for the physical and psychological challenges of operating underground.

From a building on the surface, Biashym keeps in regular contact with his men still in the pipeline. Behind him is a cabinet full of medicine.

Soldiers in the pipeline spend much of their time on their knees and suffer abrasions. Biashym admits some have had panic attacks from living in such a confined space. Others have struggled to breathe.

Hundreds of Colombian volunteers have also been involved in the operation, part of the RUG 23rd Assault Regiment.

Foreign fighters have helped boost Ukraine's depleted ranks. One of the Colombians, whose call sign is Gecko, tells me it took them 30 days to just clear 500m.

"It was difficult, it was hot and I had fear inside the pipe," he said. "But at some point I just thought, OK, just deal with it and let's advance."

Russian forces, like Ukraine's, have built fortified positions inside the pipeline. They still try to infiltrate Ukrainian positions, burrowing their way in and out of the pipe. From a control room above ground we watched Ukrainian drones target another Russian attempt to outflank them.

While some of the fighting taking place underground, there are still battles on the surface and in the air. It has been a combined operation.

But, Zanuda believes it is the best way to fight in the future. "Ground operations are now nearly impossible," he said, adding that "everyone understands, for now, the only way to fight is underground".

There'll be more missions like this, he believes. "Pipelines run everywhere," he said. "You have to remember, back in the Soviet times, oil, gas and ammonia were being transported to Europe, with the entire transit route running through Ukraine."

In reality it has been brutal, gruelling and dangerous work in the harshest of conditions.

It has taken Ukraine seven months to clear 15km of the pipeline.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has hailed it as a success. It has helped retake lost territory and been a boost for morale. But on its own it has not changed the course of the war.

For Ukraine, there is still no light at the end of the tunnel.

Additional reporting by Moose Campbell, Volodymyr Lozhko and Rebecca Hartmann

More than 200 doctors have had their details leaked to The Times newspaper

The medical regulator the General Medical Council (GMC) has apologised after it mistakenly sent information about more than 220 doctors to a national newspaper.

The information included summaries of complaints alleging antisemitism or Islamophobia against the doctors.

For some of the medics involved, it was only when the GMC alerted them to the data breach that they discovered a complaint had been made about them.

The GMC says it is "very sorry" for the incident and has reported itself to the Information Commissioner's Office.

The GMC - an independent body that regulates doctors, physician associates and anaesthesia associates to protect patient safety - sent the information about 223 doctors to a journalist at The Times newspaper.

While no names were revealed, GMC identification numbers were included, which would easily allow doctors to be found on the regulator's register.

Some doctors have also raised concerns that their ethnicity was included in the data breach.

All the medics involved have been the subject of a complaint involving either antisemitism or Islamophobia, dating from the Hamas attack on Israel in October 2023 to September 2026.

The GMC says it has a legal and statutory responsibility to investigate such claims.

Meanwhile, The Times is understood to have promised not to make any of the leaked details public, but has said it will not delete the leaked information.

A spokesman for the doctor's trade union, the British Medical Association (BMA), condemned the leak.

"The BMA is aware that a number of doctors have received communication from the GMC to say that it erroneously sent personal identifiable data about them to The Times newspaper when responding to a media request," it said.

"The GMC must take action to ensure such a breach never occurs again."

The BMA said it would look at ways to support members affected and urged them to make contact via their website.

A doctors' campaign group, The Doctors' Association UK (DAUK), called for an independent investigation into the leak.

"If a doctor sent identifiable patient information to a newspaper, they could expect to be referred to the GMC," said Dr Matt Kneale, DAUK co-chairman.

"The GMC should hold itself to the same standard of confidentiality it expects from doctors. It owes every affected doctor a clear account of what it sent, how that happened and what it is doing to get the information deleted."

The doctors' regulator says around a fifth (20%) of the complaints made have already resulted in some sanction related to antisemitism, including two doctors who have been struck off the medical register.

Just over a quarter of complaints over Islamophobia - 26% - have led to disciplinary action.

But other complaints were closed, having failed to reach the threshold for investigation.

The GMC said it had contacted the doctors affected to explain what had happened, to apologise and provide information and support.

A spokesperson added: "We recognise the concern this will cause to both those impacted personally and other registrants and we are very sorry this happened.

"Our priority continues to be supporting those affected and taking steps to reduce the impact of this incident."

An unyielding stand by its sovereignty has brought Rwanda enemies among individuals and organisations, who have always regarded having influence over the country almost as their inalienable right.

Among the organisations, none have been more virulent in their enmity than Human Rights Watch (HRW), whose anti Rwanda campaign has been so all consuming, the organisation has become inured to how it has descended into absurdity.

So egregious is HRW’s decades old anti Rwanda crusade, it earned perhaps the most excoriating, damning analysis ever levelled at an organisation of its kind, and by a career diplomat at that.

In an essay titled, The Travesty of Human Rights Watch on Rwanda , published thirteen years ago, and still freely available online, former American diplomat, Richard Johnson, forensically demonstrated how as he put it, “What Human Rights Watch (HRW) does on Rwanda is not human rights advocacy. It is political advocacy which has become profoundly unscrupulous in both its means and its ends.”

“HRW’s Board of Directors should hold Executive Director Kenneth Roth and the HRW personnel who cover Rwandan issues accountable for this travesty, which has dangerous implications for Western policy toward Rwanda and for the overall credibility of Western human rights advocacy.”

Johnson goes on to warn the organisation’s donors that they “should think seriously about what causes their money might serve. Western governments should be careful about following HRW advice, and courageous enough to challenge them publicly when need be.”

Since then, HRW has only intensified its anti Rwanda attacks, confident it seems that it can do so with complete impunity, with little to no challenge. The attacks which could never withstand close scrutiny at the best of times, have become increasingly preposterous.

There is no incident in Rwanda about which the organisation does not release a report, calling for “an independent investigation,” accusing the hugely popular government of Rwanda, of crimes against its own people, often, if not always, in contradiction to what the people themselves say.

Examples of this absurdity are legion, from the notorious claims that Rwanda was summarily executing petty thieves, only for the would be victims to emerge, asking why they were being declared dead, to blaming the government for suicides, fatal road accidents and drug addicts dying from drug overdose.

Ludicrous as they all are however, they may be surpassed by HRW latest “report,” on the awful murder of former Rwanda soldier, Sergeant-Major Robert Kabera, in Luwala, a suburb of the Ugandan capital, Kampala.

The former Sergeant-Major, fled his native Rwanda, to neighbouring Uganda, in 2020. Last month he was murdered in circumstances that are yet to be determined by police. What is known is that he was involved in disagreements with a number of individuals, and it is rumoured his murder may have been related to these quarrels.

But HRW has never allowed the absence of authoritative information to get in the way of their anti Rwanda campaign. Almost immediately after Kabera’s murder came to light, they saw an opportunity to try to link another death to Rwanda.

Their report or statement took no account of the victim’s life in Uganda, their only interest was that he had made critcisms of the government of Rwanda. That it would seem was enough for them to insinuate that Rwanda was in some way involved in the killing. They peremptorilly demanded of Ugandan authorities that they “should investigate all possible motives for the killing and take immediate steps to protect Rwandan dissidents and refugees in the country.”

And their use of the term “dissident” is worth close attention. When the description is invoked, figures like Nobel prize winning physicist, Andrei Sakharov, Nobel prize winning writer Alexander Sozhernitsyn, come to mind. Both sacrificed distinguished lives in the name of principle, and humanity’s common good.

Then we have Seargent-Major Kabera’s claims to the word dissident, or HRW’s claiming of it on his behalf. Until 2020 when he flees Rwanda, he is a member of a military band in the Rwanda Defence Force (RDF). His singing makes him something of a minor celebrity.

But he is also known to lack discipline when it comes to consumption of alcohol, which it is alleged, would bring out something rather disturbing about his make up. After one particular drinking bout, he is alleged to have sexually assaulted his own daughter, at the time only twelve years old. The allegation was in fact, rape, which in Rwanda, can carry a life sentence, if the alleged perpetrator is convicted.

Rather than face his accuser, a member of his own household, Kabera escapes to Uganda, where he asks for political asylum. Not long after that, he begins his life as a “dissident,” by creating a youtube channel, during which, in the words of HRW, he becomes “an outspoken critic of the Rwandan government.”

Predictably, Kabera was immediately embraced by the so called Rwanda National Congress (RNC), an anti Rwanda group set up by former Rwandan army General, Kayumba Nyamwasa. For the RNC, Kabera, a well known member of the RDF, will have seemed like a dream recruit. But he would go on to fall out with them, as he flirted with other anti Rwanda groups, including the unrepentantly extremist defrocked priest, Thomas Nahimana, who now comically spends much of his time selling passports, in the name of his Rwandan government in exile, on social media.

Kabera’s flight from Rwanda was not because he was an “outspoken critic of the Rwanda government,” as HRW predictably rushed to claim, but rather because someone in his personal circle, reproted him to the police, for allegedly sexually assaulting his own daughter.

In many ways however, HRW can justifiably claim credit for Kabera’s decision to opt for flight from justice rather than face his accuser in the court of law. It is unlikely that but for HRW’s decades old anti Rwanda campaign, which often fabricates imagined abuses of human rights in Rwanda, it would not have occurred to Kabera, that he could deflect attention away from his alleged crime, by claiming political asylum.

He was certain that he only had to make any claim, however ludicrous against the government of Rwanda, and HRW would be in his corner, trumpeting those claims. What he may have failed to understand however, is what Richard Johson outlined so well. The organisation has its own anti Rwanda agenda, that has little to do with human rights advocacy, and Kabera would be entertained for as long as he served that agenda.

Kabera’s journey is now reached its final destination, a sad, horrific end to a human being’s life, but for HRW, just another opportunity to demonise Rwanda, when the truth of it all is that had he stayed in Rwanda, he would have been brought to justice, and if convicted served his sentence, or his liberty returned if not.

Either way, his loved ones would have been spared the pain of contemplating what must have been horrifying last moments of his life.

Michael Duff was appointed Bradford City manager last month

Warning: This article contains references to suicide

Bradford City boss Michael Duff has praised former England and Manchester United captain Wayne Rooney for speaking out about the mental health struggles he had during his playing career.

Rooney, 41, told Gabby Logan on the Life at the Midpoint , external podcast that he was "contemplating suicide" and drinking excessively when his son Kai, now 17, was a baby.

Duff said that Rooney's comments were "important".

"People just see a superstar earning £300,000 a week and think 'it must be all right for him' - I can assure you none of our lads are earning that but they've all got their own lives," he told BBC Radio Leeds.

"Someone at that level to come out and say at the height of his fame and playing at the top level... the release is the football pitch. That's where they're happiest.

"I think it's really good what he's done, I think it's important."

During his own playing career, Duff played alongside Clarke Carlisle, who attempted to kill himself in 2014.

The former Northern Ireland international said players "weren't educated" to look for signs that team-mates were struggling at that time.

Duff said that social media brought added issues for modern players.

"Part of the job is you get stick and abuse and sometimes it goes too far," he said.

"Everyone has an opinion but you aren't allowed to have one back. They're human beings.

"I don't go on social media. If we win people will say good things, if we don't they won't.

"There's other pressure that people don't see. They see you putting on a shirt and playing in front of 20,000 which is amazing but there's loads of other pressure in that, whether it's money or providing for a family or caring for an ill parent or all these other things the outside world doesn't see."

If you have been affected by issues raised in this article, there is information and support available on BBC Action Line.

Tanzania’s national flag carrier Air Tanzania is among those not allowed to travel to European Union

Every airline certified in Tanzania and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) remains barred from operating to, from or over the European Union, after the European Commission renewed its Air Safety List as of November 2026.

The update did not add new restrictions on Tanzania or the DRC. Instead, it confirmed existing country-wide bans that apply to any carrier certified by the two countries’ aviation authorities, regardless of the airline’s size or reputation.

The Commission imposes such bans when it concludes that a state’s safety oversight is inadequate, rather than judging each airline individually.

Tanzania joined the list in June 2025, together with Suriname, after the Commission cited shortcomings in both operational and regulatory areas.

Tanzania now has the largest number of individually named carriers of any country on the list, at 34, including national flag carrier Air Tanzania and Precision Air.

The DRC follows with 13 named airlines, among them Congo Airways, Air Kasai and Air Katanga. The named carriers are examples; the ban covers every airline the two authorities certify.

In all, 154 airlines are now banned from EU skies. Of these, 126 are certified in 16 countries whose authorities the Commission says lack adequate oversight.

Twelve of those countries are in Africa: Angola, Congo (Brazzaville), the DRC, Djibouti, Equatorial Guinea, Eritrea, Liberia, Libya, São Tomé and Príncipe, Sierra Leone, Sudan and Tanzania. Angola is the only one with exceptions, for TAAG Angola Airlines and Heli Malongo.

The June revision also removed all carriers certified in Kyrgyzstan from the list, ending a ban in place since 2006. Air Express Algeria was added after the EU aviation safety agency rejected its application for third-country operator authorisation on safety grounds. It is the only Algerian carrier on the list, and Air Algérie is not affected.

The list applies to commercial air transport of passengers and cargo for hire. It restricts carriers, not people: travellers from Tanzania and the DRC can still reach Europe on approved airlines.

Banned carriers may in some cases operate through wet-lease arrangements with approved operators, under certain conditions.

The Commission describes the list as a transparency tool and a preventive measure, noting that countries under scrutiny often improve their oversight to avoid having their airlines listed.

Kyrgyzstan’s removal after two decades shows that bans can be lifted when authorities demonstrate sustained progress.

Martin Fellowes has become the youngest manager in SPFL history, taking on the Dumbarton head coach job at the age of 28.

Leaving his position as assistant manager and head of football operations at Scottish League 2 leaders Stranraer, Fellowes inherits a team six places further down the ladder.

With experience on the Scotland Under-19s coaching team, Fellowes spent almost 10 years with East Kilbride, rising from teenage kit boy to a two-month spell as interim manager in 2023, winning the Lowland League Cup.

With a day job in office furniture sales, he holds a Uefa A licence.

"You have to earn people's respect as a person," Fellowes told BBC Scotland.

"When you are a young guy and you're leading a football club, I don't think you can come in and change everything and lead with an iron fist.

"You have to get people's respect on and off the pitch. I know there will be plenty of criticism and there will be plenty of people sitting here today doubting that I'm capable of doing this job at 28.

"But now really the work for me has started on, by the end of the process, having gained those people onside to say, 'he was more than capable of doing this job and we're delighted to have him here'.

"I can only do that through winning games of football."

Martin Fellowes (right) as a 17-year-old kit man at East Kilbride

Jim Duffy was 29 when he began his long managerial career at Falkirk and Rhys McCabe was player/manager at Airdrieonians at the same age.

Ian Cathro, now leading French club Saint-Etienne, took charge of Hearts when he was just 30.

Fellowes replaces Frank McKeown, who resigned last month, while director of football Danny Lennon had been standing in on an interim basis.

The Sons are two points off the promotion places, and visit Spartans on Saturday.

"We're not going to reinvent the wheel," Fellowes added.

"We're not going to do anything that anybody else hasn't been doing.

"But if we can add the 5% to every different department and win games of football, I think over time people will understand that sometimes the age isn't a barrier but it can actually be an advantage."

Residents fled the area near Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camps following the Israeli evacuation order

Israeli ground forces have launched a rare operation in part of the central Gaza Strip outside their control, after issuing evacuation orders for residents.

Witnesses said tanks advanced east of Nuseirat refugee camp and rolled onto the territory's main north to south road under the cover of artillery strikes.

The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.

The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.

Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.

Early on Wednesday afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the incursion and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety.

It also said a section of the north to south Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.

Later, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had begun a joint operation with the Shin Bet security service "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".

"IDF troops under the Southern Command are deployed in the area in accordance with the ceasefire agreement and will continue to operate to remove any immediate threat and thwart attempts by the Hamas terrorist organisation to harm Israeli civilians or IDF troops, or to violate the agreement," it added.

Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".

Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the announcement.

In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man can be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he says.

Automatic gunfire can be heard in another video filmed just to the south-east.

A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."

"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."

A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".

Asked about reported fatalities, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.

Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.

One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second to the north in Gaza City, and the third in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.

The Israeli military said the first two strikes targeted "terrorists" and that it was not aware of the third incident, according to AFP news agency.

At least 1,658 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.

Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.

Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.

The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.

The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.

The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,700 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.
